en: 11. Sanatsujātīya-bhāṣya, composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda.
Together with the commentary composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda:
Salutation to Viṣṇu, the ancient Being, the fullness of bliss.
To the one whose light dispels all darkness, the cause of the universe.
Salutation to the teachers who are the transmitters of the tradition of the knowledge of Brahman.
A concise commentary on the Sanatsujātīya is now commenced for the easy understanding of those who desire to know Brahman.

Although the Self is by its own nature the non-dual Brahman, which is consciousness, existence, and bliss (*cit-sad-ānanda*), it is nonetheless fallen from its natural state as the non-dual Brahman-Self—due to ignorance (*avidyā*) which resides in itself and has itself as its object, which is accessible through its own experience, and which, accompanied by its own manifestation, causes one to deviate from that state. Having attained the notion of "Self" with respect to what is not the Self, such as the body and so forth, it has failed to attain [the supreme goal].

One whose human effort is futile and who has encountered every misfortune—desiring the attainment of what is desired and the avoidance of what is undesired through means fashioned solely by ignorance and karma; failing to obtain liberation, known as the supreme human goal, even when performing worldly and Vedic means; being dragged hither and thither by attachment, aversion, and other passions as if by crocodiles and the like; wandering through various species of birth divided into gods, humans, animals, and so forth; and becoming deluded while transmigrating—one somehow, by the power of merit, [attains] that which is proclaimed in the Vedas...

By performing actions for the sake of the Lord, one becomes free from the impurities of passion and the like; by perceiving defects such as impermanence, one develops dispassion toward the enjoyment of fruits in this world and the next; desiring to know the nature of Brahman as the Self—which is understood through the Vedāntas—one who is endowed with the means prescribed in the Veda, such as tranquility (*śama*) and self-control (*dama*), approaches a teacher who knows Brahman; following the teacher's guidance, through hearing the Vedāntas and other means, one realizes the truth of the identity "I am Brahman"; then, with ignorance and its effects ceased, one abides in the form of Brahman—this is the purport of the Vedāntas.
The boundary (maryādā). The Blessed Sanatsujāta will demonstrate all of this in due order.

Dhṛtarāṣṭra, tormented by grief and delusion, having heard the Vedāntic teaching that "the knower of the Self overcomes sorrow," and considering it impossible to remove sorrow without the knowledge of Brahman, spoke to Vidura: "O Vidura, if there is anything remaining unsaid by you in speech, tell it to me who am eager to hear; for you speak of wonderful things here."

And although he was learned in the scriptures, supremely compassionate, and omniscient, considering that the knowledge of Brahman pertains only to those with specific qualifications, he thought: "I am born from a Śūdra womb; therefore, I do not venture to speak anything other than this," on account of his birth from a Śūdra womb regarding the Upaniṣadic Brahman-Ātman.

Thinking, "I am not qualified for the knowledge of reality," yet considering, "How shall I establish him in the supreme state, in the Supreme Self, in full bliss and self-sovereignty through the knowledge of Brahman? and recollecting the well-known narrative from the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, he realized that no one other than this venerable Sanatsujāta would be able to show him the Infinite, the Supreme Self beyond darkness; thus, having summoned that very Lord by means of his yogic power, he honored the Blessed One with rising to meet him and other marks of respect.

"O Blessed One, there is a certain doubt in Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s mind which I am unable to express; you ought to speak to him. Upon hearing it, this lord of men shall transcend all suffering. He shall endure gain and loss, the pleasant and the unpleasant, as well as old age and death, intoxication and madness, hunger and thirst, fear and fearlessness."

"Discontent and lethargy, desire and anger, decay and rise"—O Blessed One, you ought to explain to this Dhṛtarāṣṭra that by which he may be freed from merit and demerit, the causes of all transmigratory existence, and become liberated, transcending pleasure and pain. Having been thus addressed, Vaiśampāyana said: Then the wise King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the high-souled one, having honored those words spoken by Vidura, questioned Sanatsujāta in private, desiring to hear the supreme wisdom.

Immediately after this statement was uttered by Vidura regarding Sanatsujāta, that which was spoken was honored and respected. Regarding the name "Sanatsujāta": "Sanat" refers to the eternal Brahman known as Hiraṇyagarbha; because he was well-born (*suṣṭhu jātaḥ*) from that eternal Brahman, being endowed with knowledge, dispassion, and other virtues, the Lord Sanatkumāra is called "Sanatsujāta."

In a secluded place, hidden from view and devoid of common people, that Great-Souled One of great intelligence questioned [his teacher] regarding the supreme, most excellent wisdom whose object is full bliss and non-duality. For what purpose? Desiring to become—that is, desiring to attain the Self which has been obscured by ignorance through the knowledge of Brahman.

Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: O Sanatsujāta, as for this instruction of yours that I hear—that death indeed does not exist—and that the gods and the asuras practiced celibacy for the sake of immortality: which of these two is the truth?

O Sanatsujāta, Vidura stated that what was taught to the disciples—that death indeed does not exist—was further illustrated by the fact that the gods and asuras, for the sake of immortality—that is, for the non-existence of death and the attainment of the state of the immortal—practiced *brahmacarya* and dwelt with their preceptor, such as Indra, Virocana, and others. This is heard in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, beginning with "Both the gods and the asuras understood," and continuing through the passage: "Those two [Indra and Virocana] lived for thirty-two years...

The intention is this: by the passage ending with "the two practiced the life of a religious student (brahmacarya) under Prajāpati," and by the statement, "For a hundred and one years, Maghavan indeed lived as a religious student under Prajāpati," it is shown that Indra and Virocana practiced brahmacarya under Prajāpati. If, according to your position, death does not exist, then how is it that the gods and the Asuras practiced brahmacarya for the sake of immortality? Therefore, between those two positions—whether death exists or does not exist—which is the truth? You ought to tell us that which is the truth.
The venerable Sanatsujāta said: "Some hold that immortality is attained through ritual action (*karman*), while others maintain that death does not exist at all.

Listen to me as I speak, O King, so that you may not harbor doubt regarding this. Thus questioned, the Blessed One Sanatsujāta replied: "Furthermore, some who are steeped in ignorance (*avidyā*) and who believe that death truly exists in the ultimate sense, thinking that immortality—that is, the state of being deathless—is achieved through Vedic ritual action, perform the Vedic rites for the sake of immortality, that is, for the attainment of the deathless state."

Likewise, others, blinded by the poison of sense-objects and not considering liberation—which is devoid of objects—to be possible apart from sense-objects, describe immortality, that is, the state of being deathless, as consisting in the status of gods and so forth through ritual action alone; and in that regard, they cite this verse sung by the impassioned: "Even in an empty forest of Bṛndāvana, let him wish for the state of a jackal, but never, O Gautama, for objectless liberation.
Similarly, seeing no second reality apart from the Supreme Self, they describe immortality as resulting from both knowledge and ritual action.

Others, however, who perceive the Self as non-dual and see no second entity apart from the Self, describe that there is no death, O King. Listen to my words as I speak so that the lack of contradiction between these two positions may be possible; do not hesitate—do not entertain doubt regarding the matter I have stated.
How so? Both truths are not practiced by the Kṣatriyas and others; that which is considered delusion by the seers is death.
Indeed, I declare negligence to be death, and constant vigilance I declare to be immortality. (4)

O Kṣatriya, those two aforementioned states—the existence and non-existence of death—both have been operative since the beginning; that is, they have been active from the time of the primordial creation (*ādisarga*). Alternatively, O Kṣatriya-ādi (one whose primary concern is the Kṣatriyas), they are operative in the present. But how can both existence and non-existence, which are mutually contradictory, be real? To this, he says: "Death is considered by the wise to be delusion (*moha*)."

This contradiction between existence and non-existence would arise if death were of the nature of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). What, then, is death? That which is delusion (*moha*), false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), the conceit of self in what is not-self—that is considered death by some poets; however, I do not speak of death in that way. How then? I declare negligence (*pramāda*) to be death. Negligence is a falling away [from one's true state]. (p. 193)

Because of the state of Brahman being one's own nature (*svābhāvikabrahmabhāva*). I declare that negligence—that failure to discern the Self, which is the ignorance of the Self—is the cause even of false knowledge, and is death, the seed of all evils such as birth, death, and so forth. Likewise, I declare that constant vigilance—abiding in one's own natural form—is immortality. And thus the Śruti shows that abiding in one's own true nature is itself the state of liberation: "Having attained the highest light, he emerges in his own form."
Likewise, in the *Anugītā*, it is stated clearly: "There is one sacrifice, and no second; I shall declare that which dwells within the heart.

Having sacrificed into this and swallowed all this [world], mortals become established in their own true nature. Since liberation is thus characterized by abiding in one's own true nature, and precisely because it is distinct from the fruits of the four kinds of ritual action, immortality is not achievable through action, nor through the combination of knowledge and action. Thus, it is shown that the claim made by some that "immortality is attained through action" is indeed untenable.

And he himself will state the refutation of this position: "When action arises, due to attachment to the fruits of action, people follow after them and do not cross over death; but the wise man, through knowledge, attains eternal light—for otherwise, his path does not exist. How is it understood that "negligence is death and vigilance is immortality"? To this, he says: "Through negligence the Asuras were defeated, and through vigilance the gods became Brahman.
Death does not devour living beings like a tiger, nor indeed is its form perceived. (5)

Due to negligence (*pramāda*), that is, due to falling away from their natural state of being Brahman by identifying the self with the non-self such as the body and so forth, the Asuras, beginning with Virocana, were defeated (*parābhavan*), meaning they were utterly ruined. Thus says the Śruti, starting from "not perceiving the Self" and ending with "whether they be gods or Asuras, they shall be defeated. Likewise, due to vigilance (*apramāda*), by abiding in the nature of Brahman—which is naturally consciousness, existence, bliss, and non-dual—the gods, beginning with Indra, became Brahman (*brahmabhūtāḥ*).

And thus says the Śruti: "The gods indeed meditate upon this very Self; therefore all worlds and all desires belong to them," and so forth. Alternatively, they are called *asuras* because they delight (*ramante*) in the vital breaths (*asu*), that is, in the senses alone. These *asuras* are non-knowers of the Self, worldly beings who, having transcended their natural state of being Brahman and having attained the notion of selfhood in what is not-self—such as the body and so on—come to ruin and enter the wombs of animals and other lower forms.

And so says the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "Therefore, one should not be negligent; one should not overstep this, for those of old who overstepped perished. Beginning thus, it continues: "Those three classes of beings who indeed overstepped—these are the birds, the Vaṅgas, the Aṅgas, and the Vaidehas. Likewise, those who delight in their own self alone are the gods who know the Self. And so it has been said: "Those whose delight is in the Self alone, in their own unshakable Brahman—they are celebrated as gods and as wise seers (sūris).

The meaning is that they, through non-negligence, by abiding as the self that is Brahman by its very nature, have become Brahman; that is to say, having ceased from false knowledge and its effects, they have become Brahman itself.

But surely death is well known as the one who withdraws all living beings; why then is it said, "I declare that heedlessness indeed is death"? To this he replies: "Death does not [exist]. Death does not devour—that is, consume—living beings like a tiger.
If it did devour them, its form would be perceived just as that of a tiger is; yet it is not so perceived. Therefore, death does not exist at all.

But is it not observed in the Sāvitrī episode: "Then Yama forcibly dragged from the body of Satyavān a person the size of a thumb, who had come under his control and was bound by a noose"? How then can it be said that its form is not perceived? To this he replies: "Some call Yama, others Death, others the Mind, others the Abode of the Self, and others the Immortal Brahmacarya."

In the world of the ancestors (Pitṛloka), the god Śiva rules over the auspicious ones as Śiva, while he is Aśiva (the inauspicious) over the inauspicious. This is indeed perceived as true; nevertheless, he is not Death itself. Who then is it? It is that which is called the death known as *pramāda* (heedlessness); it is ignorance (*ajñāna*) alone, because it is the direct cause of destruction.
Thus, the fact that ignorance is the cause of destruction is heard in the scripture: "If one does not realize this here... [p. 196].

"Perishing. In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, ignorance known as negligence (*pramāda*) is shown to be death itself: "Death is indeed darkness; light is immortality. Since negligence alone is the direct seed of all misfortune, therefore one should not be negligent; the meaning is that one should abide in the state of Brahman, which is consciousness, bliss, and non-dual.

Thus, the Blessed One has stated that ignorance is the cause of bondage and knowledge is the cause of liberation: "Knowledge is veiled by ignorance; thereby living beings are deluded. Since negligence is indeed death and vigilance is immortality, it follows that [liberation] is neither to be accomplished by action nor to be attained through action; for it is eternally established and eternally attained. Accordingly, the Śruti says: "This is the eternal greatness of the Brāhmaṇa; he does not increase by action, nor does he diminish."

"Only he would know its track; having known it, one is not smeared by evil action. Likewise: "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for the journey. And: "Having realized Him alone, the wise Brāhmaṇa should cultivate wisdom. Thus, it is shown that knowledge alone is the means to liberation. Similarly: "He is not grasped by the eye, nor by speech, nor by the other senses, nor by austerity or ritual action.
But when the essence of being is purified through the clarity of knowledge, then, meditating, one beholds Him who is partless."

And the Blessed One will declare that knowledge alone is the means to liberation: "O Kṣatriya, those people conquer only finite worlds through action performed," and likewise, "Knowing death to be thus born, one who stands firm in knowledge does not fear death. And so it is said in the Mokṣadharma: "A living being is bound by action, [and liberated] by knowledge.

"And one is liberated; therefore, the ascetics who see the further shore do not perform actions. And: "Knowledge is superior, for sacrifices are not so; by knowledge one crosses over the difficult passage, not by sacrifices. Thus, considering that knowledge alone is the means to liberation, the Blessed One Manu, the teacher of the Vedas, declares the abandonment of all actions: "Having set aside even those duties as they have been prescribed, the best of the twice-born should apply himself to the knowledge of the Self, to tranquility, and to the study of the Vedas."

Thus the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Sovereign, has said: "Knowledge alone, when perfect, bestows the fruit of liberation. Therefore, you must with effort understand that pure knowledge is the means to absolute isolation (*kaivalya*); it is to be heard, contemplated, and indeed perceived. For the Self is one, all-pervading, absolute, and consisting of pure consciousness; it is blissful, stainless, and eternal—this is the Sāṃkhya philosophy. This alone is proclaimed as the supreme knowledge, this is declared to be liberation, and this is described as the stainless absolute isolation (*kaivalya*) and the state of Brahman."

"Depending upon this supreme reality, established in it and having it as their ultimate goal, those great-souled ascetics, free from envy, go unto Me. Now, if this is so, then should rituals not be performed? No, they are not not to be performed; rather, they are simply not to be performed by the man of knowledge. Thus said the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva: "But for that man who rejoices only in the Self, who is satisfied with the Self, and who finds contentment in the Self alone, there exists no duty to be done. And likewise in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, the Kāvaṣeyas say: "What is there for us today..."
"What is the use of meditation? We shall perform sacrifices for the sake of wealth. "For we invoke the breath into the fire; we offer speech into the fire of the breath.
Thus it is said in the *Bahvṛcabrāhmaṇopaniṣad*: "For what purpose shall we study?"

And likewise, the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* shows the renunciation of action (*karma-saṃnyāsa*) for the knower: "Truly, the wise of old did not desire offspring, [saying], 'What shall we do with offspring, we for whom this Self is this world? They, having risen above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, then lived the life of mendicants. Similarly, in the *Laiṅga*: "For the yogi who is satisfied by the nectar of knowledge and has accomplished all that was to be done..."

"There is nothing whatsoever to be done; if there is something to be done, he is not a knower of reality. Likewise, the Atharvaṇa Śruti states: "The seer who knows this is not constrained by an injunction, for he is the creator of the word [the Veda]. By whom, then, are duties to be performed? All actions must always be performed by the ignorant person who desires to ascend [to knowledge], but not by the knower. Thus the Blessed Lord said: "O sinless one, two kinds of steadfastness were declared by me of old in this world."

"By the yoga of knowledge for the Sāṃkhyas, and by the yoga of action for the Yogis"; and likewise: "For the sage who desires to ascend to Yoga, action is said to be the means; for that same person once ascended to Yoga, tranquility is said to be the means. And so the Blessed One, the son of Satyavatī, has said: "Now, these are the two paths upon which the Vedas are established: the dharma characterized by worldly engagement (pravṛtti), and that which is situated in renunciation (nivṛtti)."

But in that case, even for those who desire to ascend [to yoga], ritual actions (*karma*) should not be performed, because actions are a cause of bondage. And so it has been said: "A living being is bound by action and liberated by knowledge.

"Even one who has committed all sins is liberated from them"—this is true. Nevertheless, actions performed for the sake of the Lord, without regard for their fruits, do not cause bondage. Thus it was said by the Blessed One: "Other than action performed for the sake of sacrifice, this world is bound by action; therefore, O son of Kuntī, perform action for that purpose, free from attachment. For what purpose, then, are they performed? We reply: for the sake of purifying the *sattva*.

And so it was said by the Blessed One: "Yogis perform action with the body, mind, intellect, and even with the senses alone, having abandoned attachment for the sake of self-purification. And: "Sacrifice, charity, and austerity are indeed the purifiers of the wise. And: "For one who is free from attachment, liberated, whose mind is established in knowledge, and who performs action for the sake of sacrifice, all action is entirely dissolved. And likewise: "Actions lead to the ripening of the impurities [of the mind], but knowledge is the supreme goal."

"When the impurity has been cooked away by actions, knowledge then arises. Now, it may be objected that even action is heard in scripture to be a cause of liberation—as in, "He who knows both knowledge and ignorance together," and "Performing actions here indeed, one should desire to live a hundred years. Likewise, Manu says: "Austerity and knowledge—both are conducive to the supreme good for a Brahmin. This is not so; this is a delusion arising from a failure to consider the preceding and following context.

For instance, after stating, "He who knows both knowledge and ignorance together," the Śruti itself demonstrates the absence of their combination by showing that knowledge and ignorance have different objects, saying, "Having crossed over death through ignorance, he attains immortality through knowledge. Clarifying this very point, the venerable Manu says: "Both austerity and knowledge bring about the supreme good for a Brahmin.

When this was said, lest there be a suspicion of a mere conjunction [of means], he showed the application of action—characterized as obligatory and occasional—to the purification of the internal organ alone, by stating: "One destroys impurity through austerity; through knowledge, one attains immortality."

Thus, having first stated that "all this is to be pervaded by the Lord" (*īśāvāsyam idaṃ sarvam*)—thereby declaring that everything is of the same nature as That—and having taught that for one who perceives everything as being of that nature, who has achieved his purpose through that very vision and perceives no further goal, the protection of the Self is accomplished through renunciation alone in the words "enjoy [the world] by relinquishing it through That" (*tena tyaktena bhuñjīthāḥ*); then, anticipating the question of how the protection of the Self is achieved for one who does not know Him to be the Self, the text says: "Performing actions here alone, one should desire to live a hundred years; thus it is with you, and not otherwise than this; action does not cling to a man. (*kurvann eveha karmāṇi jijīviṣec chataṃ samāḥ | evaṃ tvayi nānyatheto 'sti na karma lipyate nare* ||)

Since you are such a person—one who identifies merely as a human being and is ignorant—there can be no non-clinging to future karma and no destruction of past karma due to the cause of ignorance; therefore, the text shows that for the sake of purification, one who is ignorant and identifies merely as a human being must live performing action throughout his entire life, according to the injunction: "Desiring to live, let him live always performing action as long as he lives. Thus, by these statements as well, it is understood that action is merely a means to purification, not a means to liberation.

As for what was said—that from the words "by him" (*tena*) and "the knower of Brahman, the doer of merit, and the *taijasa*" (*brahmavit-puṇyakṛt-taijasaśca*), the conjunction (*samuccaya*) of these three is understood—that too must be interpreted in accordance with the application found in well-known scriptural texts. And thus, in the *Anugītā*, the Blessed Lord clearly states that action is a means to liberation only by way of purification: "Purified by obligatory and occasional rites performed without attachment to their fruits, one attains the purity of *sattva* and then becomes established in yoga (*yogārūḍha*). Then, being established in yoga...
The First Chapter:

"He goes to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. Through devotion to the guru, through fortitude, through devotion to dharma, through sacred learning, and through constant devotion to Viṣṇu, pure knowledge arises. Therefore, being devoted to dharma and endowed with faith in the Vedas, the wise man, performing his daily duties according to his capacity, attains the supreme fruits in Vāsudeva, the Supreme Self; he becomes one of pure being and is born as one established in yoga.

And the Blessed Sanatsujāta will declare that liberation has its means of accomplishment solely through the purification [of the mind]: "For that purpose, it is said that by austerity and by action, the wise man attains merit through those two; having destroyed evil with merit, he is thereafter born with his self illumined by knowledge; and by knowledge, the wise man attains the Self. Now, one might ask: how is it that liberation has its means of accomplishment solely through the purification of the *sattva*? For even without the purification of the *sattva*, liberation is indeed accomplished through knowledge alone.

True. Liberation is accomplished by knowledge alone; however, we maintain that such knowledge does not arise without the purification of the *sattva* (the quality of goodness). Thus it has been said: "Knowledge arises in persons through the destruction of sinful karma. Likewise: "In the accumulation of sins gathered over many births in the cycle of existence..."

"The mind of men, directed toward Govinda, does not arise until their [karmic] impurities are exhausted. Through austerity, meditation, and samādhi over thousands of previous births, devotion to Kṛṣṇa arises in those men whose sins have been destroyed. And so it was said by the Blessed One: "One who has attained perfection through many births then goes to the supreme goal. The yogin is considered superior to the ascetics and superior even to the men of knowledge; the yogin is superior to the performers of ritual acts. Therefore..."
"O Arjuna, become a yogi. [And: "A man attains perfection by being devoted to his own respective duty. Listen to how one who is intent on his own duty finds success:

by worshipping Him from whom the activity of all beings proceeds and by whom all this is pervaded, through his own duty, a human being attains perfection. Likewise, Yājñavalkya said: "In that state, one whose faculties are unripened is not capable of self-knowledge."

Since the attainment of the knowledge that is the means to liberation occurs only for one whose being (*sattva*) is not yet purified, through the discernment of the eternal and the non-eternal, therefore, for the sake of purifying the being, one should perform all actions—characterized by speech, mind, and body, and prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*—dedicated to the Lord of All, until, with a purified being, one becomes detached from the enjoyment of fruits here and hereafter and becomes established in yoga.
Thus the Blessed One has said: "For the sage who desires to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means," and "But renunciation, O mighty-armed one, is difficult to attain without yoga."
Its characteristic has been stated: "When one is attached neither to the objects of the senses nor to actions, having renounced all volitions, then one is said to have ascended to yoga."

Furthermore, for one whose being is thus purified by sacrifice, charity, and so forth, who has become detached from the enjoyment of fruits in this world and the next, and who is established in yoga—for him, tranquility (*śama*) alone is the cause, not action. And so it has been said: "For that very person established in yoga, tranquility is declared to be the cause. Since for one established in yoga tranquility alone is the cause and not action, therefore the yogi, endowed with the means such as tranquility and self-restraint (*śama-dama*), and possessed of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and the rest, should constantly engage himself in yoga, staying in solitude, free from expectations, with his mind and senses controlled.

"The first chapter [is for one] who has renounced all possessions. How, then, is the practice of yoga performed? Listen: having established a firm seat in a clean, level place—free from pebbles, fire, sand, noise, water-bodies, and the like—which is agreeable to the mind; having sat there upon that seat, which is neither too high nor too low and covered with cloth, antelope skin, and *kuśa* grass; and having assumed either the *svastika* or *padma* posture; holding the body, head, and neck erect and even; one should [withdraw] Viṣṇu and the other [deities] in sequence into the Full Self, which is devoid of cause and effect.

Having withdrawn [the senses] and remaining with one's whole being, one should meditate upon the God dwelling in the city (the body)—the one who is full bliss, stainless, without prior or posterior, characterized as "not this, not that," untouched by old age and the like, and established as the supreme Self whose nature is knowledge that neither rises nor sets. Thus it is said in the *Kāvaṣeyagītā* of the *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa*: "Therefore, exert yourself for liberation, by which you shall become free from suffering."

"Oṃ! Be devoted to the Praṇava, which is Brahman, the void, the supreme Pradhāna, and pure bliss. When one thus constantly unites the individual self with the Supreme Self and knows it directly, then, with ignorance and its effects dispelled, one becomes free from sorrow and has accomplished all that was to be done. And so it is said in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "If a person should know the Self, thinking 'I am this,' what desire could he have, for the sake of what object, that he should suffer along with the body?"

And so it is said in the *Īśāvāsya*: "When for one who knows all beings have become the Self alone, what delusion, what sorrow can there be for him who perceives that oneness? And likewise in the *Kaṭhavallī*: "Him, difficult to see, hidden, entered into the secret cave, seated in the abyss, the Ancient...

"By realizing the Lord through the practice of yoga, the wise man abandons both joy and sorrow; and by knowing Him as the Supreme, he is liberated from the jaws of death. "Knowing the bliss of Brahman, he fears nothing whatsoever. "The knot of the heart is severed, all doubts are cut away, and his karmas are exhausted when He, who is both the High and the Low, is realized. And so the Blessed One has said: "This is unmanifest, this is inconceivable, this is said to be immutable."

"Therefore, knowing this thus, you ought not to grieve. Having understood this, O Bhārata, one becomes wise and has fulfilled his duty. Likewise, in the *Kāvaṣeyagītās*: "One who has crossed over the sorrow of the self fears nothing—from death, from dying, or from any other fear caused by another. He is not born, nor does he die; he is neither the slain nor the slayer. He is neither bound nor the binder, neither liberated nor the giver of liberation."
This Puruṣa is the Supreme Self; whatever is other than Him is non-existent. When the noose of ignorance is burst asunder and the great doubt is severed, [He alone remains].

"When both the auspicious and the inauspicious are extinguished and the seeds of births are burnt, one attains supreme bliss—that highest state of Viṣṇu. Likewise, the Blessed Manu said: "Of all these [sciences], the knowledge of the Self is remembered as the highest; it is the foremost of all branches of learning, for through it immortality is attained. This indeed is the fulfillment of birth, especially for a Brāhmaṇa; having attained this, a twice-born man has truly accomplished his duty, and not otherwise."

Since the attainment of the supreme goal of human existence occurs through that very knowledge alone, one should know that Supreme Self, who is perfect bliss, as one's own self, thinking "I am He," and should not think of anything else. Thus says the Śruti: "The wise Brāhmaṇa, having known Him alone, should practice wisdom; he should not meditate on many words, for that is a weariness of speech. "Know Him alone as the one Self; abandon other words. "This is what must be known, eternally established in the Self; there is indeed nothing further to be known beyond this."

And likewise the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva said: "Having abandoned entirely and without remainder all desires born of volition, and having fully restrained the collection of senses by the mind itself, one should gradually attain stillness through the intellect held with fortitude; having fixed the mind upon the Self, one should not think of anything at all. Thus, as an incidental digression, the meaning of all the scriptures has been briefly demonstrated.

Now, let us return to the subject at hand: since negligence (*pramāda*) alone is the seed of all misfortune, therefore I declare that negligence is death, not Yama. However, some—blinded by the poison of sense-objects and steeped in ignorance (*avidyā*), perceiving a second entity distinct from their own Self—speak of another death, Vaivasvata, as distinct from the death called negligence which I have described; they call him "dwelling in the self" (*ātmāvāsa*), because he dwells within the self, that is, within the intellect (*buddhi*).

And so Manu said: "King Yama Vaivasvata, who dwells here within your heart—if you have no dispute with him, then do not go to the Gaṅgā, do not go to the Kurus. "Amṛta" means one whose nature is immortal; "brahmacarya" means delighting in Brahman, which is one's own true self—the sense being that he is established in Brahman. It is heard in the Kaṭhavallīs: "Who other than I could know that God, the intoxication and non-intoxication?"

Furthermore, the Lord rules over the kingdom in the world of the ancestors. How does he rule? He is *śiva* (auspicious), bestowing happiness upon the *śivas*, those of meritorious deeds; he is *aśiva* (inauspicious), bestowing unhappiness upon the *aśivas*, those of sinful deeds. Thus far, the true nature of death has been determined by the statement, "Negligence indeed is death. Now, he shows how that very [death] exists in the form of its effects: "From the mouth of men issues forth this death, which is anger, negligence, and delusion.
Moving along crooked paths through the ego-sense alone, it does not attain any union with the Self at all. (7)

That which is called negligence (*pramāda*), being ignorance (*ajñāna*) and death, first transforms itself into the nature of the "mouth" (*āsya*), which is the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) consisting of self-conceit (*abhimāna*). As it has been said: "Because it encompasses all objects, because of its connection [with them], and because of its association with the element of vital breath (*asudhātu*), the terrible quality of the Great Ego (*mahān ahaṃkāra*) is called the 'mouth'. Having thus existed in the form of the ego-sense, it then issues forth—that is, emerges—from that ego-sense in the form of desire (*kāma*).

Then, desire, as it operates within its own domain, becomes frustrated; from this, anger, negligence, and delusion arise. Subsequently, through ignorance—which has become "I-oriented," which has assumed the form of "I," and which persists as the nature of egoism—one attains identification with that [ignorance], thinking, "I am a Brahmin, I am a Kṣatriya."

Thinking "I am thin," "I am fat," "I am the son of so-and-so," or "I belong to such-and-such"—thus endowed with attachment, aversion, and other such qualities, he wanders along wrong paths, that is, paths contrary to the Śruti and Smṛti; yet he does not attain even the slightest union (yoga) with the Self, characterized by meditative absorption (samādhi). Alternatively, ignorance (avidyā), desire, and action are the causal factors of saṃsāra. In the previous passage, by the statement "that which is considered death is delusion" (moha), ignorance consisting of non-apprehension and misapprehension was described.

Later, in the section on the "arising of action" (*karmodaya*), he will explain *karman*. Now, *kāma* (desire) is being described: it is called *ākha* because by means of it living beings are cast (*asyante*) or hurled into *saṃsāra*; thus, *kāma* is *ākha*. Alternatively, it is *āsya* because it is like a mouth (*āsyavat*), since it devours the entire world. And so it has been said by the Blessed One: "This is desire, this is anger. This Death, having remained in the form of *ākha*, that is, in the form of *kāma*, then transforms into the form of *krodha* (anger). And it has been said: "From desire, anger is born."

Then, moving about through various paths by means of the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa)—which has become identified with the "I," which has fallen into egoism, and which is mounted upon the fruits of the notions of "I" and "mine"—it does not attain any yoga whatsoever with the Self.
Moreover, those deluded ones, existing here and having departed from this world, fall back again into that [state].
Consequently, the gods follow after them in confusion; thus, one encounters death through the process of dying.

Deluded by that ignorance which has transformed into the form of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth, they have been made to identify with the body and other such things as the Self; remaining under its control—that is, under the sway of death known as negligence (*pramāda*) which has transformed into the nature of egoism and the like—they, having departed from here, travel by the path of smoke and so on, dwell in that other world for as long as their merit lasts, and then fall down again to take up a body through the sequence of ether, air, rain, crops, food, semen, and blood.

And it is heard [in scripture]: "Having dwelt there for as long as their merits last, they then return again by this very same path. Thereafter, during the state of taking up a body once more, the senses (devas) follow after him and his actions (karmans); "lavante" means they flow around him completely, they revolve all about him. For this reason—namely, because of following after the qualities of the senses—he goes to death, that is, to dying. From that death, he enters another birth, and from that, again to death.

The meaning is that one who has mounted upon this continuous stream of birth and death is never liberated. Since transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) is caused by ignorance of the Self, as long as one does not directly realize the Supreme Self as one's own Self, so long does this person—overwhelmed by the threefold suffering, dragged hither and thither by passion and other afflictions like crocodiles and the like, and becoming utterly deluded—remain wandering in transmigration. This is the meaning.

Thus, the causality of ignorance (*avidyā*) and desire (*kāma*) for bondage has been stated. Now, he describes the causality of actions (*karman*) for bondage: "When action arises, those who are attached to the fruits of action follow after it and do not cross over death.
Because of the failure to realize the application of the true goal, the embodied soul proceeds everywhere through the pursuit of enjoyment. (9)

Regarding the alternative view presented—that some attain immortality through action, meaning that immortality is achieved by means of ritual works—the author refutes it: immortality does not come about through action alone; rather, when actions arise—that is, when actions are produced—those who are attached to the fruits of action follow after those very fruits. Because they follow after them, they do not cross over death; the meaning is that they continue to revolve again and again in the cycle of birth and death, which constitutes *saṃsāra*.

But why is it that, upon the arising of karma, those who are attached to the fruits of karma revolve right there? It is because they do not realize the union with the true goal (*sadarthayoga*). "Union with the true goal" means union with the ultimate reality, which is union with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). The meaning is: because of the failure to realize that union with the true goal—that is, oneness—and because of the failure to realize one's own self as the non-dual Brahman consisting of consciousness and bliss. Thus, the embodied being (*dehī*) revolves everywhere, in every direction, through the connection with enjoyment and by perceiving sense objects as mere flavors.

For just as a blind man wanders about on uneven ground, over thorns, and through rough terrain, so too does this person, devoid of discrimination, wander everywhere in pursuit of sensual pleasures. Moreover, that indeed is a great delusion for the senses; for when they are joined with false objects, his course becomes constant.
With his inner self struck by union with false objects, he dwells upon and serves sense-objects on all sides while remembering them.

The movement of the senses toward sense-objects by one who is overcome by passion is great delusion (*mahāmohana*). This is what is meant: for one who possesses the realization that sense-objects are unreal, the senses do not engage with those objects. Because there is no engagement with sense-objects, there is engagement solely with the inner Self (*pratyagātman*), and from that follows the cessation of delusion.

He who possesses the notion of reality regarding sense-objects has his senses engaged with objects that are external; therefore, he does not directly know this non-dual, internal Supreme Self as his own self. Thus it has been said: "Those whose minds are defiled by contact with the bodies of women and who are blinded by the objects of the senses do not know Brahman. Consequently, there is a great delusion in the repeated engagement with sense-objects. As the blessed Manu has said: "Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of desired objects."

"By means of the oblation, it increases all the more, like a fire with black trails. Consequently, there occurs a union with objects such as sound and so forth, which are false and imagined by ignorance; when there is this union with false objects, the course of this embodied being—the course of saṃsāra—is constant and inevitable. For this is well known: those who, failing to realize the Supreme Self who is their own self, engage with sense-objects and remain turned away from the truth, attain the wombs of animals and other such states.
And thus says the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "Those beings here... [p. 211]
"Having flowed away, these became those birds, the Vaṅgas, the Aṅgas, and the Cerapādas.

And it will be said later: "The man who follows after desires perishes along with those desires. But why is his course restricted when he is joined with unreal objects? To this he says: "His inner self struck by union with unreal objects. One whose inner self is struck—that is, whose natural state of being the Self of Brahman is struck—by contact with unreal sense-objects, remembers and worships only those objects such as women and the like, and not the Supreme Self on all sides (samantataḥ).
If it is asked, "What happens after that?", listen to what occurs there: Covetousness first strikes him down, and then desire and anger seize him.
These lead the foolish to death, but the wise cross over death through fortitude.

Covetousness (*abhidhyā*), which is the longing for objects of sense, first strikes and destroys, causing one to fall from one's true nature. Then, once struck by the meditation on objects, Desire seizes him quickly in the presence of those objects and destroys him. Next, Anger seizes him once he has been struck by Desire and destroys him. Thus, these—covetousness and the rest—deliver the foolish, the undiscriminating, and the deluded who have fallen under the sway of covetousness, desire, and anger, casting them into death. And it is heard in the *Kaṭhavallī*: "The foolish pursue outward desires... [p. 212]

“They go into the snare of Death who is spread wide; but the wise, having known immortality, do not here long for the permanent among the impermanent. However, the wise, having conquered the objects of the senses through fortitude and having realized the Supreme Self as their own Self, cross over death.
And it is heard in scripture: “Having perceived Him, one is released from the jaws of death.”

Furthermore, how do the wise, having conquered the sense-objects through fortitude, cross over death? To this he says: "He who, though not awakening to right conduct, would strike down the rising [desires] by means of contemplation—he indeed, becoming like Death itself, devours Death; for such is the one who, being thus wise, strikes down desires here."

He who, reflecting—that is, contemplating how sense objects are permeated by impermanence, impurity, and suffering—should strike down those objects that are prone to spring up (the term *utpatiṣṇavaḥ* means those whose nature is to keep leaping up and falling); he should abandon them through improper conduct, disregard, and indifference, like one who, not perceiving them as they do an impure thing, does not think of them again. That man indeed becomes the death even of Death; like Death himself, he devours Death. And it has been said: "The wise man who, through discernment, effects the withdrawal from sense objects is known as the death of Death; he is a knower of the Self and a seer."

Thus, by means of such forms as impermanence and so forth, the wise man strikes down desire through disregard and the like. But as for the one who does not strike it down through disregard and the like, what does he do? To this he says:
"The person who follows after desires perishes along with those desires."
Having cast off desires, a person shakes off whatever passion (rajas) remains.

Furthermore, he who follows after desires through longing for sense-objects perishes along with those desires; when the field of desire is lost, he perishes together with the desires. The qualities of desire are impermanent, endowed with destruction at every moment; likewise, the desirous person becomes shattered. But he who, by seeing the defects in sense-objects, does not abandon desires—having cast them out and renounced them—he shakes off, by means of discriminative intellect, whatever *rajas* characterized as merit and demerit has been accumulated here in this birth or in another birth.
But how can this body, which is so much desired, be something to be abandoned? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "This body is seen as a darkness for all beings; it is a hell.
Yet, even while running toward it, they fall headlong into a pit, clinging to it with greed."

"This body of living beings which is seen is without luster, marked by darkness, and is nothing but a hell, because it is filled with phlegm, blood, pus, worms, feces, and urine. It has bones for its pillars, is bound together by sinews, and is wrapped in flesh and blood; it is covered with skin, foul-smelling, and full of urine and excrement. Overcome by old age and grief, a dwelling place of disease, afflicted, full of passion, and impermanent—one should abandon this abode of the elements.
Thus did the Blessed Manu speak regarding the body of women and others, even though it is so utterly loathsome.

Concealing [their desires] with the notion that they are desirable, they run about, truly longing for them; they pursue them. Just as blind people, while walking, look upward and—being unable to discern a well or similar obstacle—fall headlong into such pits, so too those blinded by the poison of sense-objects, longing for women and the like, fall headlong into the very hells. This is the meaning.

He said: "The body of those who run about while thus being greedy is useless. O Kṣatriya, when someone else is not being considered, one does not study; like a tiger upon straw, that which exists within your body—driven by anger, greed, delusion, and fear—is indeed death. (15)

He who, desiring women and the like, runs after them is blinded by the poison of sense-objects; not recognizing and failing to awaken to the Supreme Self, which is distinct from those objects and constitutes his own true self, he does not study nor does he comprehend the spiritual scriptures (*adhyātma-śāstra*) concerning that Self. For such a person, blinded by the poison of sense-objects—even if he is a knower of the Vedas along with their six auxiliary limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga-veda*)—his body becomes as useless as a tiger made of straw.

And so the Lord Vasiṣṭha said: "Even that Brahmin who is learned in the four Vedas, yet does not find the subtle Brahman—he, burdened by the weight of the Vedas, is indeed a donkey among Brahmins. It is not only the body that is useless; he who is of such a nature is his very death. Thus he says: "From anger, greed, and delusion... [p. 215]

Regarding the phrase "the inner self is fear": the inner self within your body—this very self of yours that is perceived—is indeed your death, being accompanied by delusion and fear due to the two causes of anger and greed. Furthermore, he who has not conquered his senses, who is possessed of anger, greed, and so forth, and who engages with sense objects—he too is his own death, because he is the cause of his own destruction. As it has been said: "The self alone is the friend of the self; the self alone is the enemy of the self."
By what means, then, is death destroyed? To this he says: "Having thus understood death as it arises, one who is established in knowledge does not fear death;
for death perishes within his range, just as a mortal perishes upon reaching the domain of death. (16)

Thus, having understood that death—known as negligence—is born in the form of anger and other such states, and is the seed of all evils such as birth and death; and having abandoned the defects like anger which burn living beings, and having cultivated non-anger and its opposites; one who abides through knowledge as the Self that is Consciousness, Being, Bliss, and Non-dual Brahman, does not fear death. Accordingly, the Śruti says: "He who knows the bliss of Brahman fears nothing at all."

But why does one who stands in knowledge not fear death? To this he says: for that knower, when the Supreme Self—which is his own object and field—is being directly realized, the death consisting of ignorance known as negligence perishes. Just as one who has entered the domain of death, the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra), is seized by death...

A mortal who is overcome is destroyed; likewise, for one who knows the Self, the death of ignorance is destroyed when it encounters the object [of knowledge]. And it is said in the *Nāmamahodadhi*: "Established in the true state of knowledge, the fire of knowledge, the wielder of the thunderbolt of knowledge—he is renowned as the slayer of death, that hero free from envy."

Thus, having first stated that actions are the cause of bondage through the verse beginning with "In the arising of action" (*karmodaye*), it was declared that knowledge alone is the means to liberation in the verse: "Abiding in knowledge, one does not fear death. Regarding this, Dhṛtarāṣṭra raises an objection: Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: The Vedas declare here that for the twice-born, there are eternal and most meritorious worlds attained through sacrifice. They speak of these as the supreme goal. Knowing this, how indeed could one abandon action? (17)

Now, how can actions be the cause of bondage? For the Vedas, in this world-system, declare that these very worlds—attained by the righteous and virtuous through sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, which are most meritorious, pure, eternal, and extending up to the world of Brahmā—are the supreme human goal (parama-puruṣārtha). Knowing this to be the supreme human goal of the worlds, why indeed would a wise person not resort to, or practice, action as a means?
Or rather, this [p.
How is it that the knower of Brahman, knowing the action that is the means for attaining all worlds up to the world of Brahmā, does not go—that is, does not proceed—to them?

Being thus questioned, the Blessed One Sanatsujāta replied: "Thus indeed does the ignorant person wander; likewise, the Vedas speak of him who knows the true goal. He does not come here again, but as the Supreme Self, he proceeds by the right path and destroys all wrong paths. (18)

It is true that the ignorant man, blinded by the poison of sense-objects, wanders about thinking that the happiness to be achieved in the world of Brahmā and other realms is the ultimate goal; however, the wise man does not engage in those rituals which serve as the means for attaining the world of Brahmā and so forth, because he perceives defects such as ignorance (*avidyā*) in them. Thus it is said in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*: "Those worlds are called 'Joyless,' enveloped in blind darkness; to them go after death those people who are ignorant and lacking in wisdom."

Likewise, the Vedas speak of various objects and various purposes for that very person who is ignorant; because they speak only for the ignorant and not for the wise, therefore the wise person here does not enter—that is, does not engage—in the impermanent pleasures of the world of Brahman or in the ritual acts that are the means to achieve them. What, then, does he do? Having realized the Supreme Self as his own self, being the Supreme Self and being Brahman itself, he goes to the Highest. He destroys [the path] by the path. (p. 218)

And [he avoids] the wrong paths, which are the causes of saṃsāra and contrary to his own nature, consisting of the practice of dharma and adharma. Alternatively, in the reading "for thus the wise man goes around there," it means that the one who knows Brahman with attributes (saguṇa-brahma) goes around—that is, attains—the fruit of his meditation there in the world of Brahmā and so forth. Likewise, the Vedas declare this entire collection of meanings for him.

What do they say? "He does not come here"—that wise one does not come here to this world like a performer of ritual actions (*karmin*), nor is he born; rather, through the meditation on Brahman, he destroys the wrong paths that are contrary to the right path. Thus, having gone there and destroyed the wrong paths which are the causes of *saṃsāra*, being the Supreme Self, he eventually departs for the Supreme Brahman—this is the meaning.

Thus, having first shown that ignorance, termed "heedlessness" (*pramāda*), is death and that its opposite, "heedfulness" (*apramāda*)—characterized by abiding in one's true nature—is immortality through such passages as "I declare heedlessness indeed to be death," and having further shown that this very [ignorance], when transformed into the form of its effects, is the cause of all evils through the passage beginning with "From this [mouth] he issues forth" and ending with "That which is in your body is indeed death," [the text] raises the doubt: "How is there the destruction of this death? and then [proceeds with] "In this way, death being born..."

Having shown the destruction of death through self-knowledge in the passage beginning with "Knowing this, one remains by means of knowledge and does not fear death," and having raised the doubt regarding the status of the worlds of Brahmā and others as human goals in the passage beginning with "Those whom they call [attained] by sacrifice," and having stated that those [worlds] are not true human goals because they pertain to those possessed of ignorance in the passage beginning with "For thus the ignorant," liberation via the path of knowledge was taught in the words "The Supreme Self goes by the higher path. In that context, [the phrase] "The Supreme Self goes...
[is explained on page 219].

The oneness of the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para) has been stated; unable to accept this, Dhṛtarāṣṭra objects: Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Who is it that impels that unborn, ancient one? If he [impels] all this in due order, what is his purpose, or what is his happiness? O learned one, tell me all this exactly as it is. (19)

Now, if that very Supreme Self, characterized by truth and so forth, having sequentially created the world from ether down to the earth, enters into it and transmigrates by abiding in the form of the "consisting of food" (annamaya) and the rest, then who is it that yokes—that impels—that ancient, unborn one, characterized by truth and so forth, into this cycle of transmigration?

If you ask, "What is the purpose served by another [agent], since He acts by Himself?"—then what need or motive does He have for existing within various wombs? Or rather, when He exists within various wombs yet remains silent, established in His own glory, what suffering or collection of evils arises from not entering into the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*)? O wise one, tell me all this exactly as it is.

And likewise, the venerable Yājñavalkya, the foremost among the knowers of Brahman, having explained the creation of everything from that very [Brahman] and having accepted its identity as the individual soul (jīva), raised this objection: "If this is so, how is it that He is born in sinful wombs?

How is that Lord joined with undesirable states? By the words "Who impels Him?", he clearly stated the very objection raised by the disputants regarding the doctrine that Brahman is the individual soul.

[Page 220] Being thus questioned, the venerable Sanatsujāta spoke. Sanatsujāta said: "In this yoga of differentiation, there is indeed a great defect; for by means of beginningless yoga, [the qualities] become eternal. Likewise, no excess whatsoever departs from him; by means of beginningless yoga, they belong to the person."

If this is the intention of the objection—that because the distinctions of the one enjoined and the enjoiner are observed, and because such [distinctions] are impossible for a single, immutable entity, there must be a distinction [between them].

In that regard, if the manifoldness of Brahman itself were admitted, then there would be a great fault in this connection with manifoldness within the state of non-differentiation. What is the fault? Those who maintain non-duality would become proponents of untruth and non-Vedic; the heart of the Vedas and the ultimate reality of non-duality would be subverted. Furthermore, because it would have transformed into various forms, faults such as impermanence would follow, and there would result a contradiction with scriptural passages such as "not gross" (*asthūla*).

Now it may be argued: "We do not admit a plurality of Brahman; rather, we admit a distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para). Even in that case, a great fault follows: [the soul's] destruction would result. And it is heard in scripture: "For when he perceives even a slight difference in this [Brahman], then fear comes upon him"; "He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were multiplicity"; and "But he who worships another deity [thinking, 'I am one and the deity is another']... [p. 221]

The meaning is that the multiplicity of forms of the Supreme Self through Māyā is indeed logically established. And the multiplicity of forms of the One through Māyā is heard in scripture: "He became the counterpart of every form"; "Indra moves in many forms through his Māyās"; "The one God is hidden in all beings"; "That which is One, the sages call by many names"; "Being One, they fashion it as many"; "The one God has entered into many ways"; "Being One, he is divided manifold."

"You alone are He who has entered into many"; "Being unborn, He is born in many ways. Likewise, in the *Mokṣadharma*: "The one Self of all beings indeed resides in every being; it appears as one and as many, like the moon reflected in water. And likewise, Yājñavalkya says: "Just as the one ether appears distinct within jars and other vessels, so the one Self appears as many, like the sun in various receptacles of water."

And so it is said in the *Kāvaṣeyagītā*: "Just as the single sun is seen in many ways within reservoirs of water, so too the Supreme Self shines, abiding within all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Brahman stands within all bodies, both externally and internally, like space within jars; it is accessible through the intellect and not otherwise. Likewise, the Supreme Lord has said: "The Self is eternal, omnipresent, immutable, and free from defects; though being one, it appears divided through its power of *māyā* in the form of all things."

Since a single entity alone possesses manifold forms through *māyā*, therefore that very Supreme Lord, whose nature is the cause, appoints the individual soul (*jīvātman*), whose nature is the effect, by means of His *māyā* while taking into account the efforts already performed; yet, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), He neither transmigrates nor causes others to transmigrate. Thus it is said in the *Kāvaṣeyagītās*: "He is not born, nor does he die; he is neither the slain nor the slayer; he is neither bound nor the binder, neither liberated nor the giver of liberation."

"The Puruṣa is indeed the Supreme Self (Paramātman), and whatever is other than that is non-existent. Likewise, the Blessed Lord Parameśvara has said: "I am the ruler of all, by virtue of having a nature that transcends Māyā; neither does this Lord transmigrate, nor does He cause others to transmigrate. Furthermore, if a distinction caused by Māyā were admitted for this Paramātman, [it would follow that...]

Even though [the Self] exists in the form of cause and effect, its abundance—that is, the abundance of its own essential nature—does not diminish in the slightest; because the world is of the nature of *māyā*, it remains as immutable (*kūṭastha*) as before. This is the meaning. Since this is so, by means of "beginningless conjunction"—that is, through connection with beginningless ignorance—the "men," namely the individual souls (*jīvas*), become many. Alternatively, through the conjunction with the *māyā* of the "Man" (*puṃsaḥ*), the full Supreme Self (*paramātman*), which is established from time immemorial, they become many.

And so, all of this has been clearly stated in the *Anugītā*: "Existing in the form of the qualities of ignorance and in the form of reality itself, if worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) were not severed through the sense of 'mine-ness' (*mamatva*), it could not be ended in any way. Endowed with the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), one dwells within all wombs;
that which deludes all embodied beings must be abandoned by every wise man. Through its destruction, the Great Self (*mahān ātmā*) shines forth; of this there is no doubt."
For when the ego-sense is conquered, the Self will indeed be realized.
Once the self is accomplished, there will be a primordial awakening free from suffering—
the awakening that is supreme bliss, infinite, and the source of the world's manifestation.
He worships the supreme, infallible Self without deviation;
devoted to Him, through His grace, he becomes endowed with the fire of knowledge.
"Having burned away all other actions, one attains the auspicious nectar known as Viṣṇu, which fulfills all goals of perfection; such is the teaching of the Vedas.

For thus the Blessed One, the supreme teacher Parāśara, demonstrates the falsity of everything distinct from the Self: "In ultimate reality, [the Self] is of the nature of knowledge and absolutely pure."
That very [object] exists as the nature of an object due to the occurrence of erroneous perception.

Those of unawakened intellect, perceiving this entire world— which is in its true nature pure consciousness— as being composed of material objects, wander in the deluge of ignorance. But those of pure mind who possess knowledge perceive this entire world as consisting of consciousness, O Supreme Lord, as Your very form.

The Blessed One is of the nature of consciousness, for he possesses all forms as his very essence and is not a mere material object; therefore, know that the distinctions such as mountains, oceans, and the earth are but the manifestations of consciousness. However, when all karma has been exhausted and knowledge is pure, abiding in its own essential form and free from defects, then the fruits of the tree of mental construction no longer arise as real distinctions among objects.

[224] Is there any entity anywhere that is devoid of beginning, middle, and end, remaining eternally of one and the same form? O twice-born, that which undergoes change again and again is not truly so; for how can it possess reality? Earth becomes a jar, from the jar come potsherds, from the potsherd comes powder and dust, and from that, an atom.
It is perceived by people whose self-certainty is fixed upon their own karma; tell me, what is the reality here?
Therefore, O twice-born one, there is no collection of objects whatsoever, anywhere or at any time, that exists apart from consciousness;
consciousness alone is accepted as manifold by minds divided by the distinctions of their own respective karmas.
Knowledge is pure, stainless, free from sorrow, with all attachments such as defects cast away;

it is one, eternally one, the Supreme, the Highest Lord—that Vāsudeva, than whom nothing else exists. This true nature of yours has been declared by me according to knowledge, which is truth, while everything else is untrue. Furthermore, that which constitutes worldly transaction, resting upon the worlds, has also been explained to you here.
But as for the ultimate truth, O protector of the earth, listen briefly from me:
it is one, all-pervading, equal, pure, devoid of qualities, and beyond primordial nature.
For the Self is devoid of birth, growth, and so forth; it is all-pervading and immutable.

The omnipresent Lord consists of supreme knowledge and is not defined by the unreal categories of name, genus, and the like. O King, he has never been a practitioner of yoga, nor was he ever joined with it, nor will he ever be joined with it again.
For that [consciousness], though existing within the bodies of oneself and others, is indeed one and the same.
This consciousness is the ultimate reality; those who perceive duality see falsely.
This very point has been taught to you in brief, O Mahāmati.
That which is the very essence of the ultimate truth is non-dual in its entirety;
just as the single sky appears divided by distinctions such as white and blue, so too the Self, though being one, is perceived as separate by those with deluded vision.
Whatever exists here in its entirety is Acyuta; there is nothing else beyond Him.
He is I, He is you, and He is all this; abandon the delusion of duality regarding the nature of the Self.
Thus addressed by him, that best of kings, having attained the vision of ultimate reality, abandoned all dualistic distinctions;

and he too, through the awakening of the recollection of his former births, attained liberation in that very life. Viṣṇu is the stars, Viṣṇu is the worlds, Viṣṇu is the forests, the mountains, and the directions;
the rivers and the oceans—all that exists and all that does not exist is He alone, O best of brahmins.
This entire world is the expansion of Viṣṇu, who is all beings;
therefore, it should be perceived by the wise as non-different from the Self.
When the ignorance that produces the sense of difference has gone to absolute destruction,
who will create the non-existent distinction between the Self and Brahman?
Having attained the state of being that very essence, he then becomes non-different from the Supreme Self;
and any difference in him would be produced by ignorance.
"Knowledge alone is the supreme Brahman; yet knowledge is also said to lead to bondage.
All this is of the nature of knowledge, and nothing exists beyond knowledge. O Maitreya, understand that both ignorance (*avidyā*) and wisdom (*vidyā*) are indeed knowledge itself. Thus it is said.

The Lord Sanatsujāta has clearly stated this very point in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, in the context of the *Kāvaṣeya Gītā*: "Study the Vedas according to the rules, perform the prescribed rites, celebrate marriages, and worship with sacrifices; having fathered sons and reached the end of your lifespan, cast off the body through disciplined austerities. [To which they reply: "What need have we today for Vedic study, and what purpose do we serve by performing sacrifices?"

"Indeed, we call upon the vital breath in the fire; we call upon the vital breath in the fire," he says regarding speech. Having thus demonstrated the absence of any personal purpose for himself through the performance of sacrifices and other rites as a state of having fulfilled all duties, [the text continues: "But from the entrance into the house of a courtesan, there shall be a fall at the end of the merit's exhaustion."

Having shown that the world achievable through sacrifices and other means is to be abandoned—because it is marred by defects such as impermanence, as expressed in [the passage] "In the world of men there is no freedom from old age, no freedom from suffering" (*Manuṣyaloke vijarā viduḥkham*)—and having demonstrated the majesty of Truth and the other virtues in the *Yajurvedopaniṣad* starting from "Truth is supreme, the highest" (*Satyaṃ paraṃ param*), [the text concludes] with "These indeed are inferior austerities; renunciation alone excels them. Thus, [renunciation is presented] as the means for attaining the eternally established, unsurpassed bliss of Brahman, serving as its specific instrument.

In that very context, it is heard in scripture that renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is superior to all other means, such as sacrifices which accomplish impermanent results: "Not by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone some attained immortality; beyond the heavens, the supreme [state] was placed. Renunciation shines in the secret cave; those who enter it become immortal. And: "Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the realization of the Vedānta, who are self-controlled through the yoga of renunciation and are pure in being—they, at the time of the final end, are all liberated from the supreme death in the worlds of Brahman."

And likewise, the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* demonstrates the renunciation of all actions: "Having known this very Self, the Brāhmaṇas rise above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, and then lead the life of a mendicant. Similarly, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva demonstrates the renunciation of all actions: "Free from expectations, with mind and self controlled, having abandoned all possessions, performing action that is merely physical, he incurs no sin."
He who is free from expectations, pure, skillful, impartial, devoid of distress, and has renounced all undertakings—that devotee of mine is dear to Me.

He who neither rejoices nor hates, neither grieves nor desires, who has renounced both the auspicious and the inauspicious, and who is full of devotion—he is dear to Me. Equal in honor and dishonor, equal toward the factions of friend and foe, and having renounced all undertakings—he is said to have transcended the qualities.

"With intellect unattached everywhere, self-conquered, and free from longing, one attains the supreme perfection of actionlessness through renunciation. Abandoning all duties, take refuge in Me alone; I shall liberate you from all evils—do not grieve. Likewise, in the *Anugītā*, the Blessed Lord demonstrates the absence of any purpose in ritual action: "Neither a practitioner of dharma nor a practitioner of adharma, neither indeed a doer of good nor evil—he who remains absorbed on the single seat, silent, thinking of nothing at all. Thus [regarding] worldly activity... [p. 228]

"Yoga is characterized by [the performance of] signs, while renunciation is characterized by knowledge. Therefore, placing knowledge foremost, the wise man should renounce in this world. Likewise, in the Śāntiparvan, the venerable Vyāsa instructed Śuka: "A living being is bound by action and liberated by knowledge; therefore, ascetics who see the further shore do not perform action. This indeed was ordained as the way of life in the beginning by Brahmā himself."

This has been practiced by the most ancient virtuous ones, the supreme ṛṣis. One should go forth into the supreme state, the unsurpassed life of a wandering mendicant (pārivrājya). Having thus cultivated that very disposition, let it be so; and let it be heard likewise. And so the Lord Nārada demonstrates the renunciation of all actions: "Having renounced all actions, having renounced extensive austerity, having renounced various branches of knowledge, and indeed having renounced everything—this is possible for one who is liberated, who has accomplished all that was to be done in every respect."

Relying solely on alms for sustenance, one should wander in all directions; having cast off the bond consisting of the qualities (*guṇa*), having abandoned both auspicious and inauspicious karma, and having renounced both truth and falsehood, one thus becomes free from the qualities (*nirguṇa*). Abandoning all possessions, my dear, become one who has conquered the senses; abide in that state which is free from sorrow and fearless both here and in the hereafter. And thus, only for those who have renounced all action does there exist the qualification for knowledge (*jñāna*).

The Blessed Bṛhaspati said that it is not for the other: "One who has his senses extended outward is miserable; by those very same senses, when restrained, one is happy. For one possessed of passion returns to the natural state, while one free from passion attains knowledge. Likewise, in the *Aśvamedhika* [Parvan], Brahmā correctly declared to the sages that all those in the stages of life (*āśrama*) have the qualification for the renunciation of all actions: "The householder is Brahman... [p. 229]

"Whether he be a householder or a forest-dweller, whoever desires to establish himself in liberation should resort to this supreme mode of life. And: "This, they say, is the Brahmanic way of life, the singular state of happiness; this is the goal of the dispassionate, this is the eternal dharma.
Since this is so, therefore, only the renunciation of all actions (sarvakarma-saṃnyāsa) is the proper qualification for one who knows [the Truth] and for one who seeks liberation.

Thus far, the manifold nature of the one Supreme Self alone has been described through its connection with beginningless *māyā*. Now, he states that even the Lord’s status as the cause of the universe is conditioned by *māyā*: “That which the Blessed One truly and eternally creates as the universe through the application of transformation—that, I consider, is His power (*śakti*). And when there is the application of that purpose, the Vedas come into being. (21)

I consider all this to be so: that the Blessed One, who is indeed the ultimate reality, endowed with sovereignty and other attributes—that Supreme Lord—perpetually creates the universe through the process of transformation, preceded by reflection (*īkṣaṇa*) and so forth; yet it is His power, namely *māyā*, the power of the Supreme Self, which performs this, and not the Supreme Self characterized as being beyond cause and effect (*apūrva*). The meaning is that the status of being the cause does not belong to the one who is inherently consciousness, bliss, and non-dual, but rather arises through the influence of the immersion in *māyā*. If it is asked what the proof is for such a connection with this kind of power, [page 230]:

To this he replies: "In connection with that object"—that is, when there is a connection with the object of Māyā, which is the material cause of the universe for that Supreme Self, the Vedas exist. The meaning is that the Vedas serve as the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the existence of His Māyā. And thus says the Śruti: "Indra (the Lord) appears in many forms through his Māyās"; "From him, the Master of Māyā, he creates this entire universe; but [know] the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā"; and "The divine power of the Self, veiled by its own qualities. Likewise, the Blessed Vāsudeva said: "For this divine Māyā of mine, consisting of the three qualities (*guṇa*), is difficult to overcome."

"Though I am unborn and my nature is imperishable, though I am the Lord of all beings, yet by presiding over my own material nature (*prakṛti*), I manifest myself through my own power of illusion (*māyā*). Under my supervision, material nature produces the world of the moving and the unmoving. And likewise: "This is your *māyā*, which utterly deludes those who do not know its true nature; by it, the fool ascends to the notion of the Self in that which is not the Self. This is the profound *māyā* of Kṛṣṇa, the creator of this universe, by which the world is constrained in the relationship of the supported and the supporter."
"Oh, how difficult to cross is this most profound illusion of Viṣṇu!
Bewildered in mind by it, one does not know the Supreme Lord."

Thus, having first demonstrated the nature of death through such passages as "I declare negligence indeed to be death," its persistence in the form of its effects, and the manifold evils caused by it; and having raised the doubt, "By what, then, is this destroyed? and shown that the attainment of fearlessness comes from the knowledge of the Self alone through such passages as "Knowing death thus as it is being born, one who stands firm through knowledge does not fear death"; and having resolved the two incidental objections—Dhṛtarāṣṭra speaks in order to gain a thorough understanding of the nature of action:
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Since some here practice righteousness and others here practice unrighteousness, is righteousness struck down by evil, or does righteousness strike down evil?

Since some in this world practice dharmas such as the *agnihotra* and others likewise practice non-dharmas, does their dharma get destroyed by the sin? Or rather, does the dharma destroy the sin? Or perhaps, due to their being of equal strength, there is the destruction of one by the other? [The answer is: For the ignorant person, there is indeed the experience of both; there is no destruction of one by the other.

But for the wise man, there is the destruction of both by the fire of knowledge; thus Sanatsujāta gives the answer: "Established in that [Self], the wise man indeed constantly destroys both through knowledge, for this is established. Otherwise, the embodied soul incurs merit; likewise, he incurs sin, for this is established. (23)
Being thus questioned, the Blessed Sanatsujāta replied:

"Even though situated in that action consisting of merit and demerit, and even while performing both types of action characterized by merit and demerit, the wise man constantly and invariably destroys—that is, annihilates them—by means of knowledge. How is this understood, that the wise man destroys them through knowledge? To this he says: For this is established and well-known in the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas. And so the Śruti says: 'The knot of the heart is severed,' and so forth."
