"Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows this"; "Just as the tuft of a reed-stalk thrown into a fire is consumed, even so all his evils are consumed"; "Thus the knower, having shaken off both merit and demerit, stainless, attains the highest equality"; "Having shaken off evil like a horse shakes its hair"; "As a well-kindled fire reduces fuel to ashes, O Arjuna."

Now, if on the other hand the embodied soul, being devoid of knowledge, attains merit, it likewise attains demerit [regarding the Tathāgata] and experiences its fruit. If it is asked how this is understood, he says in response: "This is indeed established and well-known in the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, Purāṇas, and so forth. And thus says the Śruti: "Thinking that sacrifices and charitable works are the highest, the deluded know no other good; having reached the sixth heaven by their merit, they enter this world once again."

"Blissless indeed are those worlds, shrouded in blind darkness; to them go after death those people who are slayers of the Self. Likewise, Vāsudeva says: "The knowers of the three Vedas [worship Me]," and "Having enjoyed that vast heavenly world..."

[233] Is it that both [results] are experienced by the ignorant man, or that one is destroyed by the other? To this he says: "Having gone, both the unstable fruit of good and evil action is enjoyed; however, the wise man here drives away evil by means of merit (dharma). Know that for him, dharma is more powerful. (24)

Having gone to the other world and attained both results achievable through merit and demerit, one experiences that which is characterized by merit and demerit as impermanent. And it is heard in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka: "O Gārgī, he who, not knowing this Imperishable, offers oblations in this world... and so forth.

"Now, those who know otherwise than this have other rulers and belong to perishable worlds"—thus it is said in the *Chāndogya*. And that wise man (*vidvān*) also, by means of action (*karman*) performed in accordance with righteousness (*dharma*), drives away—that is, destroys—evil; here in this world, the "wise man" is one possessing the characteristics about to be described, who knows how to apply [the teachings] and performs actions for the Lord. And so He will say: "For that purpose, austerity has been declared, as well as sacrifice; through these two, the wise man attains merit."

"Having destroyed evil through merit, he is thereafter born with his self illumined by knowledge. Through knowledge, the wise man attains the Self; otherwise, one who merely desires the fruit of heaven takes all that was performed here, enjoys it there, and returns again to the path. "For those who have a competitive rivalry regarding dharma, that is not a means for realizing that [Self]. For those who have no [rivalry] regarding dharma... [p. 234]

"And competition among them is the means for attaining that knowledge. Know—that is, understand—that for the wise person who thus understands this application and performs action for the sake of the Lord, merit (dharma) is more powerful than sin. However, for the mere performer of ritual action, it is not more powerful; for him, there is simply the experience of both, and the destruction of one by the other does not occur.

To whom, then, is [the path] a means for attaining heaven and the like, and to whom is it a means for attaining knowledge by way of the purification of the mind? To this, he says in two verses: "Those for whom there is rivalry regarding their duties, as if they were powerful men contending in strength—those Brāhmaṇas, having departed from here, go to heaven and attain radiance. (25)
For those who have no rivalry regarding the Dharma, that is the means to their knowledge;

they are Brahmins liberated from this world and go to heaven, the triple-heaven (triviṣṭapa). [Page 235] For those who are devoted to sense-objects, there exists a rivalry or competition regarding Dharmas such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice—which serve as the means for attaining things like Urvaśī—because they hear of the enjoyment of Urvaśī and others during their residence in heaven, thinking: "By performing a Dharma superior to this one, may I become even happier than he."

Just as among the strong there is a rivalry—just as when one sees a powerful king, the thought arises, "By attaining power even greater than his, and by conquering him, may I become happier than he"—so it is here. Those Brāhmaṇas who are entitled to perform sacrifices, being attached to the fruits of their actions, go from this world after death by the path of smoke and so forth, and reach the heavens, attaining the state of luminosity in the form of stars and the like.

And it is heard [in scripture]: "Now, those who worship with the thought, 'This is the sacrifice and the pious work, this is what has been given,' they pass into smoke," beginning thus, and continuing: "This is King Soma; that is the food of the gods, which the gods consume. Having dwelt there until the exhaustion [of their merit], they then return again by this very same path."

For those whose minds are not drawn toward sense objects and who feel no rivalry or competition regarding dharma—such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, which achieves impermanent results—the performance of action for the sake of the Lord, without regard for its fruits, makes that very action, such as sacrifice, a means to knowledge by way of purification. And the Blessed One himself will state that it is a means to knowledge precisely through the door of purification: "Having destroyed sin by means of merit, he thereafter becomes one whose self is illumined by knowledge."

Those Brāhmaṇas whose inner being (*sattva*) has been purified by sacrifices and other means, who realize the Supreme Self as their own self—they, having departed from this world characterized by cause and effect, being liberated, attain and reach Brahman, which is full bliss and characterized by heavenly happiness. He states its distinction from the other [ordinary] heaven with the word "Triviṣṭapa. It is called *triviṣṭapa* because it protects (*pāti*) that which is freed from the three—whether the three internal and external afflictions, the three qualities such as *sattva*, or the three states such as waking—or because it protects the qualified person who has entered those [states]. Alternatively, it is *triviṣṭapa* because it protects the one who has entered (*viṣṭam*) by those [three].

Now, regarding the conduct of the learned Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya— who, having renounced all ritual actions while still remaining within the life of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), has performed the hearing of the Vedānta and other duties, and is established in his own greatness— the people who know the Vedas declare his perfect conduct as follows:
"One should not regard him too much as either an outsider or an insider."

People learned in the Vedas declare the perfect conduct of that wise man who has become dispassionate: one should not regard him as a mere yogi; he should contemplate extensively—meaning much—the external and internal objects of attachment, such as sons, friends, wife, and so forth (the latter being "internal," the former "external"). The meaning is that he remains entirely beyond their reach, in such a way that sons, friends, and others do not grasp hold of him.
Regarding what kind of place his residence should be, he says: "In whatever place one might think there is an abundance of grass and water, as in the rainy season..."

A Brahmin should live on food and drink, and he should not be distressed by it. In whatever place—such as a region free from the afflictions of wild animals—he considers food, drink, and so forth to be most abundant and plentiful, just as grass and water are found in abundance during the rainy season; some say "tṛṇolapa" refers to the rice and other foods fit for sages, citing the phrase "tṛṇolapa is known among the rice and other foods consumed by sages," while others say it is a specific kind of venerable *dūrvā* grass. Staying there, he should subsist upon that food, drink, and so forth.

He should not be distressed—that is, he should not become agitated—lest he be tormented by the thought, "How indeed will the maintenance of the body be accomplished in a place devoid of food, drink, and the like? For from that, the attainment of yoga would not occur. Regarding this, the author says that one should dwell even near such a person: "He who, when one does not speak to him, bestows upon him inauspiciousness and fear, as if doing something excessive—he is superior, and not the other kind of person."

In whatever place, for the teacher who is a wandering mendicant of the highest order (paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka-ācārya)—who does not speak, remains silent, conceals his own greatness, is covered by anything whatsoever, eats anything whatsoever, sleeps anywhere at all, regards the Self alone as the world, and moves about like one who is dull-witted, mute, a child, or a ghost—anyone may bring about inauspiciousness and fear, or bestow misfortune, contempt, and the like.

Likewise, one who acts as if he were "excessive"—that is, a person who, knowing the characteristics of one whose wisdom is established and recognizing him as a knower of Brahman, does not offer worship appropriate for a knower of Brahman (such as prostration, salutation, and so forth), but instead treats him with contempt and the like—such a person is superior to this wise man, and not the other who worships him with prostration and so forth, regarding him as the Lord. Thus said the Blessed Manu: "From honor, O King..."

"A learned Brahmin should recoil from it as if from poison, yet always desire it as if it were nectar. Thus spoke the venerable Parāśara: "Since honor causes the supreme ruin of the perfection of yoga, the yogi who is disregarded by people attains the success of yoga. What kind of food, then, should be eaten? To this he says: "He whose self would not be distressed when his faults are being spoken..."
One should not harm the property of a Brahmin; that food is approved by the virtuous.

Or, he who, having made a complete withdrawal from one who does not speak but remains silent, established in the nature of full bliss, would not cause him mental distress or torment, nor would he violate the property of a Brahmin—meaning he would not damage the grass mat, deerskin, kuśa grass, books, and so forth, which are the instruments for the practice of devotion to Brahman—it is said accordingly: "They do not call jewels, gold, and the like the 'property' of this yogi; they know that the kuśa grass, bark garments, cloth, and so forth, belong to the yogi as his 'Brahma-property'."

Furthermore, he should not harm any property belonging to a Brahmin or the possessions of a Brāhmaṇa; his food is considered acceptable as food to be eaten by the virtuous. Again, he describes his proper conduct: "A Brāhmaṇa should always live in a state of unrecognized life; even while living among his kinsmen, he should not acquire anything at all."

A Brahmin who knows Brahman should think: "I must always, as a matter of rule, practice living in ignorance and live in concealment. While dwelling in the midst of his kinsmen—sons, friends, wife, and so forth—he should not perceive or recognize anything at all; some say this means even his own dog. The meaning is that the yogi, having renounced sons, friends, wife, and the like, should remain solely established in the Self and live in concealment. And thus says the Śruti: "The family, sons, and wives, and the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences in their entirety..."

"Having abandoned sacrifice and the sacred thread, the sage wanders in secret. Likewise, the venerable Vasiṣṭha said: "He whom no one knows as either existing or non-existing, as unlearned or deeply learned, as well-behaved or ill-behaved—he is a Brāhmaṇa. Even though he knows, the wise man should conduct himself among people like one who is dull-witted. The point is that liberation, characterized by the attainment of steadfastness in knowledge, belongs only to such a person and not to another, because of the latter's abundance of distractions.

Alternatively, "I must constantly practice my conduct—characterized by steadfastness and meditative absorption—in Brahman, which is unknown to the senses, beyond the range of sight and other faculties, inexpressible by words, abiding as the nature of knowledge that neither rises nor sets, untouched by hunger and other such afflictions, whose essence is perfect bliss, the innermost of all, and the indwelling Self; I must not practice it in that which is external, such as the body, senses, sons, friends, or wife, thinking, 'I am fat,' 'I am thin,' 'I go,' 'I stand,' or 'I am impotent,' 'I am one-eyed.'"

A Brahmin who knows Brahman should think: "I am mute, I am deaf; I am the son of so-and-so, the grandson of so-and-so; I am a Brahmin, I am a Kṣatriya; my wife, my son, my wealth, my affectionate kinsmen and friends"—thus he should not form such notions regarding the Self. And so says the Śruti: "That which the eye does not see, that by which the eyes see—that alone is Brahman. Since one must thus remain steadfast in Brahman while it remains unknown, therefore, among kinsmen, there are defects such as anger and pride, as well as sense-objects and the senses.

"these indeed are declared to be your kinsmen, O embodied one"—since the senses and so forth have been designated by the word "kinsmen," while dwelling among the senses and so forth—seeing, hearing, touching, breathing, moving, eating, thinking, and even knowing—one should not perceive or realize the Self in the form of the knower and so on, because the Self is the witness of all that. Thus says the Śruti: "Now, he who knows 'let me smell this,' he is the Self.
The meaning is that one should not grasp the two bodies and their attributes as the Self.
But why is it not grasped in this way? To this he says: "For what Brāhmaṇa would deign to think thus of his inner self?"

[One realizes] the signless, immovable, pure [Self], which is devoid of all dualities. For who indeed [could realize] the Self—the innermost one, the witness of the knower and so forth—which is signless (nirliṅga), devoid of the gross and the subtle, immovable, empty of action, agent, and so forth, pure (śuddha) being free from the defect of ignorance, devoid of all dualities, and free from such attributes as hunger, thirst, grief, delusion, old age, death, cold, heat, pleasure, and pain; [the Self] which is not an object of the means of knowledge in the manner described above, [namely] by way of the two bodies and their attributes?

The meaning is that one who thinks, "I am fat," "I am thin," "I am going," "I am seeing," "I am mute," "I am deaf," "I am one-eyed," "I am happy," or "I am miserable," does not deserve to be considered a Brāhmaṇa; for if that were the case, his very status as a Brāhmaṇa would be lost. And the author will say later: "He alone who does not deviate from the Truth is to be known by you as a Brāhmaṇa."
But he who thinks thus is the most wicked, as it is said: "He who represents himself as something other than what he truly is—
what sin has not been committed by that thief who steals his own self?"

He who perceives himself—though he exists otherwise as the Self that is consciousness, signless, stainless, pure, free from all dualities, and as the non-dual Brahman consisting of consciousness, existence, and bliss—as being otherwise, namely as the two bodies and their attributes, thinking "I am the doer, I am the enjoyer, I am happy, I am miserable, I am fat, I am thin, I am the son of so-and-so, the grandson of so-and-so, I am a Brāhmaṇa, I am a Kṣatriya"—what has not been done by that fool, that non-knower of the Self, that thief of the Self, that robber of the Self?

"Sin" means that all [sins], beginning with the great transgressions (*mahāpātaka*), have been committed by him alone. And so says the Śruti: "Sunless indeed are those worlds, enveloped in blind darkness; to them go after death those people who are slayers of the Self. Likewise it has been said: "Having attained the status of a Brāhmaṇa in this world, one may not be mute or deaf; yet such a person, a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa, does not escape from *saṃsāra*."

Therefore, the meaning is that one must abandon the sense of self-identity with the body, senses, and so forth—which have become objects of perception—and instead practice steadfast devotion toward the Supreme Self alone, which is unknown and beyond the reach of speech and other faculties.
Otherwise, what happens to one who does not perceive the body, the senses, and their attributes? To this he says: He would be unwearied, a non-appropriator, esteemed, and free from affliction;
though learned, he would not be like those who are merely learned. He is a Brāhmaṇa, a knower of Brahman, a seer. (34)

He who is a non-appropriator—that is, one who does not appropriate as the self the body, the senses, and their attributes, which are not the self—that person would be unwearied; he would not be joined with the fatigue of saṃsāra. For hunger and so forth are attributes of the body and its like. And thus says the Śruti: "Hunger and thirst belong to the vital breath (prāṇa); grief and delusion belong to the mind; old age and death belong to the body."

For when there is the superimposition of the two bodies, there occurs the superimposition of their attributes. In this way, one becomes free from affliction through the absence of weariness. Anger, joy, greed, delusion, and so forth are obstacles and afflictions (*upadrava*). One who is devoid of these is "free from affliction. He is esteemed as a refined person (*śiṣṭa*) by the wise; he should not act like one who is not refined, nor should he behave like a fool. A Brāhmaṇa who knows Brahman is a seer (*kavi*).
Now, censuring those who act without concealment, he says: "Those fools who always consume what has been vomited do so for their own misfortune;
in this way they consume what has been vomited by partaking of their own semen."

Based on the observation that "the fool is called a child (bāla), and the dog is also remembered as a child," just as children or dogs, being foolish, eat what has been vomited or regurgitated, so too those who are supposedly learned knowers of Brahman, proclaiming their own greatness and behaving in an unhidden manner, eat what has been vomited or regurgitated by consuming their own power. That this eating of the vomited leads only to misfortune and not to well-being—this is the meaning. Therefore, being firm, one should conduct oneself exactly like one who is not learned.
[243] Now, praising the yogin, he says: Those twice-born ones who are poor in human wealth but rich in the Vedas—know them to be invincible and unshakable; they are the very body of Brahman.

Those twice-born ones who are not wealthy in human riches—such as wife, sons, and property—but whose selves are unattached; who are instead "wealthy" in the Vedas, that is, in the means of practice such as non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, non-possessiveness, celibacy, and meditative concentration taught by the Vedas—they are invincible and unshakable. One should know them as the very body of Brahman; the meaning is that one should know them as having become the essential nature of Brahman.
Moreover, this is the majesty of the knower of Brahman: no one here can rival that brahmin, by whom every god who performs the sacrificial tasks is known, and toward whom he himself exerts effort.

They are called *sviṣṭakṛt* because they perform the sacrifice (*sviṣṭa*) well for all [deities], beginning with Agni. Thus says the Śruti: "Performing the well-sacrificed, he is the *Sviṣṭakṛt*. One should know that for the purpose of relinquishing [the offering] by designating each of the deities individually, no one here—even if he is a sacrificer to all the gods—is equal to a Brāhmaṇa; the meaning is that he is not equal to a Brāhmaṇa who knows Brahman.

This is not surprising: even that specific deity for whom the sacrificer himself exerts effort for the sake of a fruit by means of the renunciation of the oblation intended for it—thinking, "This is for Agni; this is for Indra"—that specific deity who is the recipient of the oblation is not equal to the knower of Brahman; how much more so, then, can it be said that the sacrificer, who is but a beast for the gods, is not his equal? And thus it is stated in the *Mokṣadharma*: "He does not even stand in comparison with a Brāhmaṇa; how much less so [with one who knows Brahman]! He is merely sacrificed to. (p. 244)
"By which mantra the best of the twice-born becomes a sacrificer. And so said the blessed Manu: "There is no being in this world superior to those who know Brahman."

Furthermore, he describes the conduct of that very person: "But when one who does not strive for honor is honored, let him, being thus honored, not think highly of himself; nor should he be distressed when not honored."

If certain wise men—who know the characteristics of one whose intellect is steady—recognize and honor that knower of Brahman, who is effortless, who has withdrawn all beings into his own majesty, who is established in his own greatness, who practices celibacy and so forth, who has performed renunciation, who has well-ascertained the meaning through the realization of Vedānta, who is a teacher of the Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka order, and who moves in secret; if they honor him, thinking "This is he," then that wise man, being honored by them, should not think "I am being honored."
Remaining thus, people, perceiving him as dull because he is unacquainted with social graces, treat him with contempt; regarding that cause of contempt, he should not dwell upon it nor feel remorse.
How, then, should one behave when honored and when insulted? He says this in two verses: "The world always acts according to its own nature;
'the wise honor him here,' thinking thus, he is honored."
Thinking, "The fools who know not the Dharma, being shunned by the world, will not honor those worthy of honor," one should remain unhonored.
When it is said that "the wise honor the knower of Brahman," one should consider this to be their natural disposition, like the opening and closing of an eye— a spontaneous activity inherent to them.

Likewise, when insulted and treated with contempt by people, the wise man should think thus: "The ignorant, who do not know what is unrighteous, who lack discrimination, and who are devoid of both worldly wisdom and sacred scripture, will not honor that which is worthy of honor; they will not even honor that which is truly honorable. He should consider this to be the very nature of the foolish. Thus the wise man remains unhonored and unpraised. Now, he explains that honor and silence have different spheres of application: "Honor and silence never dwell together.
This is indeed the sphere of honor, while that is the sphere of silence; so the wise know."

Indeed, worldly knowledge (*māna*) and silence (*mauna*) do not dwell together in one place. For this world, which is perceived through direct perception and other means of knowledge, is that which is "seen" (*lokyate*); thus, the meaning is that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is the object of worldly knowledge. That "other world" is the domain of silence. What is that? It is "That" (*tat*), the name of Brahman. As the Blessed One has said: "The designation of Brahman is traditionally held to be threefold: *Oṃ*, *Tat*, and *Sat*. Likewise, in the *Anugītā*: "*Oṃ*, *Tat*, and *Sat*—these indeed bestow union with Viṣṇu and other [liberations]."

That Brahman is indeed inexpressible; the meaning is that it is the object of *mauna* (silence/contemplation). This is what is being said: from *māna* (pride/desire) comes the attainment of saṃsāra, while through *mauna* comes the attainment of Brahman. And it has been stated in the *Hairaṇyagarbha*: "Attachment to the enjoyment of food, women, and so forth is known as *māna*; that which is the cause for attaining the bliss of Brahman-joy is known as *mauna*."

Now, he demonstrates the absence of liberation when there is association with honor and wealth: "For prosperity indeed arises from association with honor and wealth, and that prosperity, moreover, is an obstacle."
O Kṣatriya, the sublime state of Brahmā is extremely difficult to attain for one who is devoid of wisdom.

O Kṣatriya, for one who dwells for the sake of honor, who lives amidst the objects of human pride, who revolves within the manifold conceptualizations of the sphere of honor, and who performs rituals that serve as the means for attaining heaven, cattle, food, and so forth—that person, blinded by the poison of sense-objects, indeed acquires prosperity (*śrī*). Yet even that prosperity is an adversary, an obstacle on the path to the highest good (*śreyaḥ*). Thus it is said in the *Mokṣadharma*: "This delight in dwelling in a village is a binding rope; those of virtuous deeds go forth having cut it, but those of evil deeds do not cut it."

For that fool who, thus overcome by worldly glory, engages with sense objects—he, being devoid of wisdom and devoid of knowledge, finds the Brahmic glory characterized by the bliss of Brahman to be very difficult to attain. As it is said in the *Hairaṇyagarbha*: "That which is eternal, consciousness-bliss, devoid of qualities and forms, known as Bliss, supreme and pure—that is called the Brahmic Glory. And she is very difficult to attain; she cannot even be heard of [by the unqualified]. Thus says the Śruti: "He who is not obtained even for hearing by many..."
Now he shows the gateways for entering the splendor of Brahman:
"The wise declare that there are many kinds of gateways, which are difficult to traverse."
Truthfulness, honesty, modesty, self-control, purity, and knowledge—these six are the obstacles to pride and delusion. (43)
Thus ends the first chapter in the venerable Sanatsujātīya.

The virtuous rightly declare that the gates for the entry of the splendor of Brahman (*brahmalakṣmī*) are manifold and difficult to practice—that is, they involve painful conduct. What are they? Truth and uprightness: truth is speech consistent with reality and beneficial to living beings; uprightness is freedom from crookedness. Modesty is shame regarding the performance of what should not be done. Self-control, purity, and knowledge: self-control is the cessation of activity of the internal organ (the mind); some say it is the cessation of the external organs. Purity is the washing away of impurities. Knowledge is the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).
These six are the obstacles caused by pride and delusion. Thus ends the first chapter of the *Sanatsujātīyabhāṣya*.
