O King, since the Vedas do not enter into that [Reality] along with the mind, therefore there is silence regarding it;
yet where this sound of the Veda has arisen, that [Reality] shines forth as being identical with it.

Because the Vedas, together with the mind (*manas*), do not penetrate this Supreme Self (*paramātman*); as the Śruti says: "From whence words turn back, together with the mind, having failed to reach it. For that very reason, that Supreme Self, which is beyond the range of speech, is *mauna* (the state of silence).

If this is so, then what are the characteristics of the Supreme Self? To this he says: "That from which the Vedic word has arisen. This means that Brahman is the cause of the scriptures and so forth, being the objective ground (nimitta) upon which the Vedic word arises. Alternatively, it means that the Vedic word is employed as a designator, having arisen within that which is called consciousness (saṃvedana).

Thus, this Supreme Self, whose nature is consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpa*), is what is expressed by the word "Veda. If the Supreme Self is beyond the range of words, how can it be understood that the Supreme Self is of the nature of consciousness? To this he says: "O King, that Supreme Self shines for us as consisting of that [consciousness], that is, as consisting of light (*jyotirmayatvena*). The meaning is that such is our own experience; one should not entertain doubt in this matter. Alternatively, He is perceived as consisting of light in the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, *Itihāsa*, *Purāṇa*, and so forth. And thus says the *Śruti*: "The gods [know Him] as the light of lights..."

"Indeed, within the body there is that bright one consisting of light, whom the ascetics who have destroyed their defects behold. And likewise the Blessed One said: "He is called the light even of lights, beyond darkness."

Now, in order to fully understand the nature of the Vedas, Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: "That twice-born man who studies the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, and the Sāmaveda—does he not remain unstained even while committing sins, and is he not smeared by sin?"

The intention [of the questioner] is this: "Is one who, while committing sins, studies the Vedas such as the *Ṛgveda*, purified by that Vedic study, or not? You ought to tell me this. Being thus questioned, the venerable Asita Sanatsujāta replied: "Neither the Sāman, nor the *Ṛc* verses, nor the *Yajus* formulas, O wise one, can cleanse this person from sinful action; I do not speak falsely to you."

If one who commits evil deeds studies the Vedas, such as the *Ṛgveda* and others, those Vedas do not protect—that is, they do not shield—him from sinful action for being a practitioner of forbidden acts. I am not speaking falsely; this is exactly so, and no lack of confidence should be placed in this. This is the meaning.
If it is asked what they do, he says in that regard:
"The Vedic hymns do not rescue one who is deceitful and who acts with guile from evil."
Like birds with grown wings leaving their nest, the Vedas abandon him at the time of death. || 5 ||

The Vedas do not rescue—that is, they do not protect—this person from evil and unrighteousness: one who is an atheist, a doer of sin, one who has merely studied the Vedas, one who has studied the meaning of the Vedas, a deceiver, a hypocrite, one who lives by deceit, or one of false conduct.

If it is asked, "What will they do?"—just as birds with fledged wings abandon their nest, which is their own refuge, so too at the time of death, the Vedas abandon this person, who was their own support; the meaning is that they no longer serve his human purpose.

When this had been said, Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke: Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: "O wise one, if the Vedas are not capable of protecting the knower of the Vedas, then why is this eternal proclamation of the Brāhmaṇas [still maintained]?"

Since, by the passage beginning with "At the rise of karma," it has been shown that obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*) actions are causes of the world of transmigration (*saṃsāra*) by being the means for attaining the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*) and so forth; and since it has been shown that prohibited action is a cause of evil by being the cause of hell—if the Vedas are not capable of protecting the knower of the Vedas, then for what reason is this [claim] an ancient (*sanātana*)—meaning traditional—prattle? The meaning is: because they are causes of the evils of transmigration, the study of the Vedas, the inquiry into their meaning, and their performance should not be undertaken.

This would be mere idle chatter if this alone were the meaning of the Veda; rather, the supreme human goal known as liberation (*mokṣa*), distinct from heaven and the like, is the true meaning of the Veda. As for ritual action and meditation, they are taught by the Veda only because they serve that [liberation] indirectly, being means to the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-śuddhi*), which is itself a means to the knowledge that leads to its attainment. For instance, the Veda reveals that very Supreme Self, the supreme human goal: "Blissless indeed are those worlds, shrouded in blind darkness."

"Those ignorant and undiscerning people go to those [worlds] after death. Having thus shown that the worlds such as heaven are not the ultimate human goal and lack the nature of bliss because they are the domain of those possessed by ignorance, [the text] shows the state of one who has accomplished all that was to be done through the knowledge of the Self: "If a person were to know the Self, thinking 'I am this,' desiring what, or for the sake of what longing, would he suffer along with the body? Having shown this, it further says: "Being right here, we know that; if we have not known it here, there is a great destruction."

"Those who know this become immortal, while others enter only into suffering"—having thus shown that those who know the Self attain immortality, whereas those who do not know the Self suffer the destruction of the Self and encounter misfortune; and having repeatedly demonstrated its true nature, the vision of its meaning, and its fruits through such passages as, "When one perceives this very Self as the immediate God, the Lord of what has been and what is to be, one does not shrink away from it," [the text asks: how is it that this [Self], being dragged hither and thither by passion and the like as if by crocodiles and other [sea monsters]?

Thinking, "I shall liberate the evildoer who is overwhelmed by sense objects and establish him in the supreme state—the sovereign kingdom of liberation known as the full bliss of the Supreme Self"—the scripture enjoins sacrifices and other duties as the means for the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), which is itself the means for the knowledge that is the instrument for attaining that [liberation], stating: "Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas, through sacrifice, through charity, through austerity, and through fasting. Therefore, it is precisely because they serve that purpose [of liberation] that sacrifices and the like constitute human goals (*puruṣārtha*).
Otherwise, however, in the case of heaven and so forth, they would lack the status of a human goal, just as the Śyena sacrifice and others do.

Because they are the cause of the misfortune of saṃsāra. And thus says the Śruti: "Trivial and indeed unstable are these forms of sacrifice, eighteen in number, among which action is the highest; those fools who rejoice in this as the highest good, they surely return again to old age and death."

Since the Vedas are thus the cause for the cessation of the miseries of saṃsāra by means of teaching liberation and its means, they are indeed capable of protecting those who know the Vedas. With this entire point in mind, he says in three verses; therein, with the first verse, he shows the Supreme Self, the supreme goal of man, which is eternally immediate: Sanatsujāta said: O Great-souled One, it is through the specific forms of names and so forth belonging to Him alone that this world shines. Having pointed Him out correctly, the Vedas speak of Him, and they proclaim His absolute difference from the universe. (7)

O noble one, this world shines through the specific forms of names and so forth, which are imagined by the *māyā* of that very Supreme Self. How is it understood that this world shines through the specific forms of names and so forth belonging to that very Self? Having pointed out the manifold forms created by *māyā* in the words, “Indra, by means of his *māyās*, assumes many forms,” they declare his true nature in the instruction: “This is that Brahman—without prior, without posterior, without interior, without exterior; this Self is Brahman, the experience of all.”

The Vedas [teach this]. Thus, by stating, "There are indeed two forms of Brahman: the formed (mūrta) and the formless (amūrta)," and so forth, the Vedas first indicate that the very nature of the world consists of these formed and formless aspects, which are like the Self; then they declare its true nature through such passages as "Not this, not this" (neti neti). Likewise, by indicating that everything from space down to the earth is the effect of that very [Brahman] in the passage, "From the Self, space was produced," and so on, the Vedas then declare its true nature by means of the presentation of the sheaths (kośa), using such passages as, "From which words turn back, along with the mind, having failed to reach it."

With the passage beginning, "‘Teach me, O Venerable One! and he approached him," the scriptures point out that very Self—starting from name and ending with the vital breath—as the world produced by its own māyā; then, with the passage beginning, "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else, that is the Bhūman," the Vedas proclaim its true nature as the Infinite (Bhūman), situated beyond darkness in its own glory.

Not only do the Vedas proclaim this, but the sages as well describe that Brahman as *viśvavairūpya*—that is, having a form contrary to the forms of the universe. Thus the venerable Parāśara said: “That which has all distinctions subsided, which is pure existence alone, beyond the reach of the mind, yet to be realized by the self through the self—that knowledge is designated as Brahman. And that is the supreme form of Viṣṇu, called the formless (*arūpa*), unsurpassed; it is characterized by being the opposite of the universal form (*viśvarūpa*) of the Supreme Self.”

Now, by means of two verses, he demonstrates that actions performed for the sake of the Lord possess the status of human goals (*puruṣārtha*) through a traditional succession by way of the purification required for the knowledge that is the means to attaining Him; whereas other [actions], being causes of the misfortune of *saṃsāra*, lack the status of human goals. To that end, it is said: "Austerity and sacrifice are declared for that purpose; through these two, the wise man attains merit (*puṇya*). Having destroyed evil (*pāpa*) by means of merit, he is thereafter born with his self illumined by knowledge."

Through knowledge the wise man attains the Self, and not otherwise, even if he desires the fruits of the [other] goals of life. Whatever is performed here, having grasped all that, one enjoys it there; yet again, one returns to the path.

That Brahman which is of a nature opposite to the manifold form (of the world) has been declared by the Veda for that purpose. What is it? It is austerity (*tapas*), such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances; and sacrifice (*ijyā*), such as the *jyotiṣṭoma*. If one asks what results from these, [the answer is: through those two—sacrifice and austerity—that wise man, who knows the aforementioned application and performs action for the sake of the Lord, attains and reaches merit (*puṇya*).

He becomes conjoined with the *apūrva* (unseen merit) produced by his action. By means of that merit, having struck down and exhausted his sin, he subsequently—after all impurities have been exhausted—is born with a self illumined by knowledge. He becomes one whose nature is the non-dual Brahman, which is consciousness, eternal bliss, and is revealed by knowledge. Through knowledge, the wise knower of the Self attains and reaches the Self, the Supreme Self. Otherwise, however, by not performing actions for the sake of the Lord, one whose impurities have not been exhausted does not become a knower of the Self.

Then, desiring the fruits of the constituent groups (*varga*), desiring the fruits of the senses (*indriya*), and desiring the fruits such as heaven, one takes up all that was performed in this world—such as sacrifices—and enjoys its fruit in the other world, the hereafter. Thereupon, by means of the remainder of one's karma, one returns again to the path, the path of *saṃsāra*.
Thus says the Śruti: "Having dwelt there for as long as the [accumulated] momentum lasts, they then return again by this very same path."
Now, with reference to the wise and the ignorant, he describes the disparity in the fruits of actions: "In this world, austerity is practiced, yet its fruit is enjoyed elsewhere;
for Brahmins, austerity is highly potent, while for others, it is only to that extent."

It is common to all that the fruit of whatever austerity (tapas) is performed in this world is enjoyed in the other world, yonder; however, for Brāhmaṇas who know Brahman, there is this distinction: their austerity becomes exceedingly prosperous—that is to say, it becomes a cause for the increase of its fruit. And so says the Śruti: "Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the Upaniṣadic insight, that alone becomes more powerful."

For others who do not know the Self and are attached to sense objects, that [result] is indeed not fully realized; the meaning is that whatever fruit is heard to result from a particular action, that action is merely a means to obtain that much fruit and does not become a cause for the full perfection of the fruit.
Having heard this, Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke: Dhṛtarāṣṭra said, "O Sanatsujāta, tell me how austerity alone becomes exceedingly abundant; O Lord, how may I understand this?"
This is straightforward.
Thus questioned, the Blessed One spoke; Asanatsujata said: "They declare this to be stainless austerity alone.
When this is fully perfected, it becomes true austerity, and not otherwise. (12)

That which is this stainless austerity (*tapas*) is called "the absolute" (*kevala*); it is said to be the "absolute seed. That which is the seed and the cause of this entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is called the "absolute. As Āhośanā says: "The reality established in the equilibrium of the qualities (*guṇasāmya*) is called the 'absolute'; from this absolute, this world, consisting of both the existent and the non-existent, has arisen. This very austerity becomes perfected and exceedingly abundant only when it is stainless, and not otherwise. [p. 260]
It does not become defiled; then it becomes exceedingly prosperous and does not fail.
He praises this very point: "O Kṣatriya, all this that you ask me has austerity as its root;
through austerity, those who know the Vedas attain the supreme immortality. (13)
The meaning of this verse is clear.

Having heard this, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: "Tell me of the blemish of austerity; I have heard of austerity that is stainless. O Sanatsujāta, tell me by what means I may know this secret, eternal [truth]."

"It is said that 'this austerity alone is stainless'; O Sanatsujāta, tell me of the stain of that austerity which has been heard of, so that by means of that stainless austerity we may know this secret, eternal Brahman."

Thus questioned, the Blessed One replied; Sanatsujāta said: "O King, those twelve defects beginning with anger, as well as the seven acts of cruelty, and those twelve qualities beginning with knowledge which are known in the scriptures as the expansive virtues of the twice-born—"

[Page 261] O King, anger and the other twelve are the defects of that austerity; likewise, there are seven acts of cruelty which are the defects of that austerity. Furthermore, there are twelve qualities such as knowledge and others, which are expanded and taught in the scripture—the Vedic tradition—as virtues for the twice-born; it is my intention to explain both these virtues and these defects. He shows anger and the others: Anger, desire, greed, delusion, the desire to know, compassion, envy, pride, sorrow, longing, jealousy, and contempt—these twelve must always be avoided by a man of great virtue. (16)

Anger (*krodha*) is that which arises from the obstruction of desire; it is the cause of beating, reviling, and so forth, as well as a causeless agitation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), characterized by symptoms such as perspiration and trembling of the limbs. Desire (*kāma*) is the longing for women and other objects. Greed (*lobha*) is the craving for another’s property, as well as the inability to employ one's acquired wealth for a worthy purpose (*tīrtha*). Delusion (*moha*) is the state of being devoid of discrimination between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done. The desire to know (*vivitsā*) is the wish to experience the flavors of sense-objects. Cruelty (*akṛpā*) is harshness.

Envy (*asūyā*) is the revelation of faults in those who possess virtues; it is characterized by intolerance toward the virtues and other qualities of others. Pride (*māna*) is the high estimation of oneself. Sorrow (*śoka*) is a distraction of the internal organ born from separation from a desired object, characterized by weeping, brooding, and so forth, and having no remedy. Desire (*spṛhā*) is the longing for the enjoyment of objects. Jealousy (*īrṣyā*) is the inability to endure the prosperity of others. Disgust (*jugupsā*) is [the aversion toward... [p. 262]

The desire to disparage virtues, or loathing—these faults such as anger and the like, which are impurities of austerity, should always be avoided by one possessing the great quality of Brahman. For Brāhmaṇas, the possession of superior qualities is established by their very nature. Thus it has been said by the Blessed One: "Tranquility, self-restraint, austerity, purity, forbearance, and uprightness, as well as knowledge, realization, and faith in the Vedas—this is the action pertaining to a Brāhmaṇa, born of his own nature."

Alternatively, "Mahāguṇa" means one who has attained Brahman; the meaning is that [these states] should always be avoided by one endowed with that great quality characterized by the attainment of Brahman. And it is said in the *Nāmamahodadhi*: "He is called 'Mahān' (the Great One) because he is greater even than the great; and one who is joined with the qualities for attaining Him is remembered as 'Mahāguṇa'."
He states the reason why these must always be avoided: "O King of kings, each one of these attends upon a man, seeking an opening like a hunter among deer."

Just as a hunter, seeking the interval or opening among deer and intent on searching for a weak point, follows after them, and having found that opening, kills them; so too do these things—anger and the rest—intent on searching for the weaknesses of those people, attend upon each individual person. Alternatively, there is the reading "they attend upon people" (*manuṣyān paryupāsate*); in that case, the construction is that they attend upon each person individually. And thus, having found a weakness, they destroy them. Therefore, even one among these... [p. 263]

A fault (*doṣa*) is a cause of destruction; since this is so, the meaning is that they must always be avoided. And it is said in the *Hairaṇyagarbha*: "Just as for a traveler in the wilderness, lions, tigers, wild beasts, and the like are sources of affliction, so too are anger and other evil qualities for human beings. Now he describes the seven types of cruel persons (*nṛśaṃsa-saptaka*): "One who increases enmity through the awareness of shared enjoyment, one who regrets what has been given, the miserly, the weakling, one who praises his own group, and one who hates his wife—these others are the seven forms of cruelty. (18)

He whose consciousness is occupied with *saṃbhoga*—that is, the enjoyment of sense objects—is one whose awareness is fixed on such enjoyment. "Increasing like poison" (*viṣamedhamānaḥ*) means increasing by causing affliction to others, just as poison does; or alternatively, there is a variant reading, *dviṣamedhamānaḥ*, meaning increasing by performing hateful actions through which he prospers by way of those very acts against living beings.

One who regrets what has been given (*dattānutāpī*) is he who, having previously given wealth and so forth with a sense of righteousness, later becomes tormented, thinking, "Why did I give this? A miser (*kṛpaṇaḥ*) is one who, out of greed for even a mere fragment of wealth, endures all forms of humiliation. One who is weak (*avalīyān*) is devoid of the strength of knowledge. One who praises the group (*varga-praśaṃsī*) is one who praises the group of sense organs. And one who hates his wife (*vanitā-dveṣṭā*) is he who hates his own wife when she has no other refuge. These seven, distinct from the previously mentioned [faults] such as anger, are of the nature of cruelty (*nṛśaṃsa*).

[264] Now the twelve qualities beginning with knowledge are described: knowledge, truth, self-control, sacred learning, lack of envy, modesty, forbearance, and freedom from deceit; sacrifice, charity, fortitude, and tranquility—these are the twelve great virtues of a Brāhmaṇa. 19.

Knowledge (*jñāna*) is the realization of the true nature of reality. Truth (*satya*) is speech that corresponds to the facts and is beneficial to living beings. Self-restraint (*dama*) is the subduing of the mind. Learning (*śruta*) is the study of the scriptures concerning the inner self (*adhyātma*). Freedom from envy (*amātsarya*) is the absence of intolerance toward all beings. Modesty (*hrī*) is shame regarding the performance of improper acts. Forbearance (*titikṣā*) is the capacity to endure the pairs of opposites (*dvandva*). Absence of malice (*anasūyā*) is the non-exposure of the faults of others. Sacrifice (*yajña*) refers to the *agniṣṭoma* and other rites, as well as the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*). Charity (*dāna*) is the relinquishing of wealth and other possessions to Brahmins. Fortitude (*dhṛti*) is the restraint of the senses even when objects of sense are present.

*Śama* is the cessation of the internal organs; some say it is the cessation of the external organs. These [virtues], beginning with knowledge (*jñāna*), are the great vows (*mahāvratas*) belonging to the Brāhmaṇa, serving as the means for attaining the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Those twelve "non-spreading" [vices] beginning with ignorance (*ajñāna*), which were introduced previously in the phrase "those twelve non-spreading [vices]," have now been described. Now he offers praise for these virtues: "But he who would live apart from these twelve [vices] might rule this entire earth.
One who is endowed with three, two, or even one of these, becomes distinguished in succession, becoming truly silent (*maunabhūta*). (20)

But he who does not depart from these aforementioned qualities—that is, who remains endowed with them—shall rule over this entire earth; he governs it and brings it under his own control. Those among these who are not separated from three, two, or even one, or who are endowed with at least one of them, become progressively distinguished knowers of reality; having become silent, they become Brahman.
Now he describes the faults of self-restraint (dama) in three verses: "That [restraint] would have eighteen faults; it becomes adverse when something is done against one's will:
falsehood, calumny, thirst, hostility, pride, and discontent."
Worldliness, pride, dispute, injury to living beings,
slander, excessive speech, remorse, intolerance, and lack of fortitude;
Failure to achieve one's goals, sinful deeds, and violence—these are proclaimed [as the faults].
He who is free from these defects is called "self-controlled" (dama) by the virtuous. Self-control would be characterized by eighteen faults; it becomes possessed of eighteen faults.
If it is asked why these are considered faults—it is because they become adverse when acted upon.

When any one of these is committed, it becomes an act contrary to self-restraint (*dama*). What are they? Falsehood is speech that does not correspond to reality. Slander is speech intended to defame others. Craving is the desire for sense objects.

Contrariety is being adverse toward all things. Darkness is ignorance. Discontent is lack of satisfaction with what has been obtained; or alternatively, delight is attachment to the enjoyment of women.

Hatred of the world is the practice of causing distress to people. Arrogance is the state of not bowing down to anyone. Quarreling is the practice of engaging in strife with others. Cruelty to living beings is the harming of creatures for the sake of filling one's own body. Slander is the proclamation of another's faults in their presence.

Excessive speech (*ativāda*) is meaningless prattle; remorse (*paritāpa*) is the futile brooding over suffering; intolerance (*akṣamā*) is the inability to endure dualities; lack of fortitude (*adhṛti*) is fickleness regarding the objects of the senses; failure to achieve accomplishment (*asiddhi*) refers to the lack of success in virtue, knowledge, and dispassion; sinful action (*pāpakṛtya*) is the performance of prohibited deeds; and violence (*hiṃsā*) is unrighteous injury. Thus, these faults of self-restraint (*dama*) have been proclaimed. That quality which is free from these defects, such as falsehood and the rest, is called self-restraint (*dama*) by the virtuous.
Now he describes the faults of intoxication: "Intoxication has eighteen faults, and renunciation is of six kinds;
these reversals are known as the faults of self-restraint (dama) that have been illustrated."

Arrogance (*mada*) consists of eighteen faults, and renunciation (*tyāga*) is of six kinds. These opposites—beginning with falsehood and ending with violence—which were previously recorded as the faults of arrogance, are here recorded as opposites; they are declared to be the antidotes to arrogance, consisting of truthfulness and so forth, and are the destroyers of arrogance. What are they? Truthfulness, absence of backbiting, lack of craving, freedom from hostility, absence of darkness, lack of discontent, freedom from hatred toward the world, absence of pride, non-contentiousness, non-violence toward living beings, absence of slander, absence of excessive speech, absence of causing distress, forbearance, steadfastness, success, absence of evil deeds, non-injury, and compassion—these are declared to be the destroyers of arrogance.
It was stated that "renunciation is of six kinds. Regarding this, he says: "But the superior renunciation is of six kinds; among them, the third is difficult to perform.
By means of that [third], they indeed cross over suffering; when that is abandoned, all is conquered."

But renunciation is of six kinds; among these six types of renunciation, the third is difficult to perform and hard to accomplish. By means of that third renunciation, one indeed crosses over suffering—divided into internal and other categories—and when that renunciation is performed, everything is conquered.
He demonstrates the sixfold renunciation: that which consists in giving one's sons and wealth to a worthy petitioner;

the second is the performance of sacrifices and works of public utility (*iṣṭāpūrta*) through the constant application of dispassion (*vairāgya*); and the third, O King of kings, is known as the renunciation of desire. One should be vigilant by means of these [six]; and that [state] is considered to possess eight qualities.

[268] To give wealth and sons to one who is worthy—an Arhat—who asks for them: this pair of renunciations (*tyāga*) is the first among the six. The second would be *iṣṭāpūrta*: that which is given in the context of Vedic rites (*iṣṭa*) and that which is given in the context of Smārta rites (*pūrta*). Some say that *iṣṭa* is what is given to the gods, and *pūrta* is what is given to the ancestors.

O King of kings, the third is traditionally known as the renunciation of wealth and the like, as well as the renunciation of desire, by one who has attained constant dispassion (*vairāgya*), who perceives defects such as impurity and impermanence in the elements of existence (*sattva*), and who, through that detachment, abandons riches and so forth.

To the question "What is gained by these?", he says: "The heedful one. For those who are heedful, desire does not decay. It is said in the *Rājadharmas*: "Dharma has malice as its stain; wealth has concealment as its stain; desire has heedlessness as its stain; yet when free from that, it increases virtue. One who is endowed with these six kinds of renunciation would be heedful. That heedful person becomes possessed of eight qualities, being endowed with eight virtues.
Who are they? He shows them: truthfulness, meditation, concentration, inquiry, and indeed detachment; non-stealing, celibacy, and likewise non-possessiveness. (28)

Truth (*satya*) is speech that corresponds to reality. Meditation (*dhyāna*) is the continuous, uninterrupted flow of the mind toward some auspicious object of focus, such as the *maṇḍala-puruṣa* or others, like a stream of oil. Concentration (*samādhāna*) is the state of abiding as the Self—which is Brahman, naturally consciousness, existence, bliss, and non-dual—after having performed the withdrawal of the universe and all else by means of the *praṇava*. The inquiry (*codya*) is: "Who am I? To whom do I belong? From where [do I come]? (p. 269)

"Or," and so forth. Detachment (*vairāgya*) is the absence of craving for objects perceived through the senses or heard of in sacred tradition. Non-stealing (*asteya*) is the non-theft of one's own property or that of others. Self-theft has been described thus: "He who represents himself as something other than what he truly is. Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is the renunciation of the eightfold sexual act. As it has been said: "Remembering, praising, playing, looking, secret conversation, [accepting gifts, longing, and union]."

"Intention, determination, and the actual accomplishment of the act—wise men declare this to be the eightfold sexual union. Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is the opposite; it likewise possesses these same eight characteristics. Non-attachment (*asaṃgraha*) means non-possession of children, wife, fields, and so forth. One should protect these [virtues].
"One should avoid these faults," he said; thus the faults of self-restraint have been described, and one should completely abandon those faults.
In the abandonment of faults, there should be vigilance, and that is considered to possess eight qualities.

One should avoid those defects which have been stated [in the rule] that "there should be no lack of vigilance" (mo'pramādaḥ). Why? He says: because when those defects are abandoned, one will not be negligent; this is the meaning. Furthermore, that vigilance is considered to have eight qualities, since it was already indicated previously by the passage beginning with "truth, meditation," and so forth. This is the meaning.
Now the praise of truth is being performed: "O Indra among kings, become one whose self is truth; the worlds are established upon truth.
They call those who speak the truth formidable, for immortality is placed within truth."

"O Indra among kings, become one whose self is truth, whose very nature is truth; for all worlds are established upon truth. They say that these worlds have truth as their mouth, truth as their chief, and that the attainment of their very existence depends upon truth. Indeed, immortality is placed within truth; by 'immortality' is meant liberation. "One should practice the vows of austerity here with faults entirely withdrawn. This alone is the wealth acquired through night and day; truth is indeed the best among the virtuous."

Being free from the previously mentioned defects by means of the very cessation of those faults—such as anger and the like—one should practice the vow of austerity here. This, which was ordained by the Creator, the Supreme Lord, is indeed the truth and the best for the virtuous.

Now, with the words "how is it exceedingly prosperous?", he concludes the matter introduced [earlier]: "But when it is free from these defects and endowed with these qualities, this asceticism alone becomes exceedingly prosperous. (32)

But that austerity which is free from these aforementioned defects such as anger and the like, and is endowed with these qualities such as knowledge and so forth, becomes solely and exceedingly prosperous.
What need is there for much? O Indra among kings, I shall tell you in brief that which you ask of me:
it is pure, it removes the sins accumulated in the home, and it wards off birth, death, and old age. (33)
O Indra among kings, that which you ask me, I shall tell you this in brief and in summary; what is about to be spoken is sin-destroying, pure, and removes birth, death, and old age.
If it is asked what that is, he says this: "O Bhārata, if one is liberated from the five senses, from the mind itself, and from the past and the future, he shall become happy."

O Bhārata, if one is liberated from the five present senses along with their objects, as well as from the mind regarding both the past and the future, he would be happy; the meaning is that he would indeed be liberated.
When this had been said, Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke: Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: "Most people say that one should speak using narratives as the fifth [Veda];
likewise, others are masters of four Vedas, and still others of three. (35)

"Those who know two Vedas, those who know one Veda, and others who know the Anuvākas—among these, tell me who is the Brāhmaṇa whom I should recognize as such. Those for whom the Purāṇa is the fifth among the Vedas are called *ākhyānapañcamas*. As it is heard in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "Itihāsa and Purāṇa are the fifth.
By means of those Vedas, with the Purāṇa as the fifth, he is most abundantly—that is, exceedingly—spoken of and praised.

"He thinks highly of himself, [saying], 'I am superior to all. Some read "is called" (*kathyate*). The meaning is that a certain person is called "one who knows the five Vedas" (*pañcavedī*) by means of the Vedas and the fifth, the narrative texts (*ākhyāna*). Likewise, others know four Vedas, others three, others two, and others one; and still others are those who have abandoned the *Ṛgveda* and the other Vedas. Among these men, tell me of one who is superior and most excellent, whom I may know as a true Brahmin.

Intending to show that he alone is a *brāhmaṇa* who abides as the Self of Brahman—which is by nature consciousness, eternal bliss, and non-dual—and to demonstrate that everything other than him is rooted in ignorance of that [Brahman], he says: "O King of kings, it was from the ignorance of the one Veda that those many Vedas came into being; while Truth is one, O Indra, only someone rare is established in Truth."

Of the one Veda—the meaning is that of the single, non-dual consciousness whose nature is pure awareness (*saṃvidrūpa*), wherein this object of knowledge (*vedya*) is of the form "this" and the form "not-this," and the knowing itself (*vedana*) is the Veda—due to the lack of comprehension of that one Veda, which is Brahman, the Vedas such as the *Ṛg* and others became many. Here, the Vedas such as the *Ṛg* and so forth, by performing inquiry for the sake of realizing that [Brahman], obtained the designation "Veda. Alternatively, they are called "Vedas" because they establish existence (*sadbhāva*). Or, they are "Vedas" because they know, being the means for the act of knowing.

Alternatively, the Vedas are so called because they cause one to obtain the Self which is dependent upon Brahman; or, the Vedas are so called because they are the means for obtaining Brahman as one's own Self. [The roots] *vida* in the sense of "investigation," *vida* in the sense of "existence," and *vida* [in the sense of "knowledge"]...

Because these roots—*vid* (to know) and *vidl* (to obtain)—function within their respective domains, they are therefore called *veda*. If one asks what the nature of that single Veda is, the answer is from the Śruti: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite. Therefore, because of the lack of realization of the Truth—which is Brahman, the nature of the single Veda—the Vedas have been explained as being many; all the Vedas are the means for perceiving its meaning. O King of kings, having understood this, do you yourself abide in that very Brahman? Or is there someone else who is established and firmly rooted in the Truth?
Listen further from me: he who knows this becomes wise and ever remains in truth;
for it is only out of greed that giving, study, and sacrifice proceed. (38)
For what purpose? If not, then hear what happens there: for those falling away from truth, their intentions become false; consequently, action expands out of a lack of firm grounding in truth. (39)

For those falling away from Brahman—characterized by truth, knowledge, and so forth—and having abandoned their innate state of being Brahman, they have instead attained the notion of a self in the non-self, such as the body and other such things; their volitions become false, that is, they become futile, because they are innate...

The meaning is that false intentions and the like do not succeed; consequently, ritual action such as sacrifice would expand and proliferate. All of this occurs because of the non-determination and non-comprehension of Brahman, which is characterized by truth and so forth, since saṃsāra has its cause in the ignorance of the Self. As long as one does not directly know the Supreme Self as one's own Self, for that long—overwhelmed by the threefold suffering and being dragged hither and thither by passion and other afflictions like crocodiles—one remains deluded, possesses false intentions, and persists in the means for attaining heaven, cattle, food, and the like. This is the meaning.
Now he describes the characteristics of a Brāhmaṇa: "One who has studied many words and is eloquent is called a Brāhmaṇa;
however, he alone who does not deviate from the truth should be known by you as a Brāhmaṇa."

One who recites much—that student of the five Vedas including the narrative texts (*ākhyāna*)—should be known as "one of many words," but not as a true *brāhmaṇa*. If one asks, "Who then is the primary *brāhmaṇa*?"—the meaning is: he alone who does not depart from the Truth characterized by truthfulness and so forth, but remains always established in his own natural state as the non-dual Brahman-Self, which is eternal bliss. He alone is to be known by you as a *brāhmaṇa*, and no other; namely, one who, having fallen away from the Truth and remaining unfulfilled, engages in ritual action.

And thus the Śruti shows that only one who knows Brahman is a Brāhmaṇa: "Having fully understood both silence and non-silence, he is then a Brāhmaṇa; he is a Brāhmaṇa," and also, "Free from evil, free from passion, and free from doubt, he becomes a Brāhmaṇa."

[275] This might be so if that very Brahman were established; yet it is not established, because the Veda is intent upon something else. To this, he says: "O Best of Bipeds, the Vedas (Chandāṃsi) exist there by means of their own inherent power (svacchanda-yoga);
therefore, those noble ones who know the Vedas, having studied them, have indeed gone beyond the Veda to what is to be known. (41)

He, the best among bipeds, [is the one] in whom the *chandāṃsi*—the Vedas—exist by virtue of their own free application; "free application" (*svacchandayoga*) means independence (*svādhīnatā*), that is to say, according to His will. They exist in Him, the Supreme Self; they find their authority in Him alone. And it is heard in scripture: "That goal which all the Vedas proclaim," and also, "By all the Vedas, I alone am to be known."

The meaning is that since the Veda culminates in the goals of human life (puruṣārtha), and because everything other than that—being impermanent, impure, and permeated by suffering—lacks the status of a human goal, the authority of the Vedas consists in their teaching the nature of those goals, the knowledge thereof, and the means to attain them.

Since the Vedas serve as the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding that very Supreme Self through the application of their own inherent power, for that reason, the noble ones—the learned knowers of Brahman—having studied and mastered those Vedas and having performed such acts as listening to the Vedānta, have reached and attained the true nature of the Supreme Self, which is of the essence of consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpa*), and not the world of manifestation (*prapañca*) which is an object of knowledge. If this is so, then, regarding the fact that the Veda is the means of knowing it, [the Upanishads state]: "That is indeed other than what is known, and furthermore, it is other than what is unknown.

Fearing that this might contradict such Vedic scriptures as, "From whence words return, together with the mind, not having attained [it]," he says: "There is no one who is a knower of the Vedas; by means of the Veda they do not know the Veda, nor do they know the object of knowledge (vedya).
He who knows the Veda also knows the object of knowledge; but he who knows the object of knowledge does not know the Truth. (42)

Among the Vedas, such as the Ṛgveda and others, not even one Veda is the knower of the Supreme Self, who is beyond the reach of speech and whose nature is pure consciousness. Why? Because by means of the Veda—consisting of the Ṛgveda and so forth, which is insentient—they do not know the Veda, that is, the Supreme Self whose nature is consciousness; nor do they know the world of manifestation (*prapañca*), which is the object of knowledge, for all establishment depends upon consciousness.
Since all establishment depends upon consciousness, therefore he who knows the Veda—that is, the Supreme Self whose nature is consciousness—he indeed knows this entire world of objects of knowledge.

And so says the Śruti: "Verily, my dear, by the seeing, hearing, and realizing of the Self, all this is known. He who thinks "I know the object of knowledge" does not know, he does not understand the Truth characterized by reality and so forth—the Supreme Self. Now, one might raise the objection: "In that case, by saying 'By means of the Veda they do not know the Veda nor the object of knowledge,' you are asserting that for those who do not know the Self, the phenomenal world (prapañca) is simply non-existent. Anticipating this, he says: "He who knows the Vedas also knows the object of knowledge; those who know the Vedas do not know it, nor do the Vedas. [p. 277]
Nevertheless, those Brahmins who know the Veda through the Veda become knowers of the Veda.

He who knows—that is, understands—the Vedas, such as the Ṛgveda and others, and he who knows that which is to be known (the Vedic content), even he is one who does not know the Self; for by means of a differentiated consciousness, he knows only the phenomenal world (prapañca) which is an object of knowledge. Now, one might raise the objection: "If that is so, then he should likewise know the Supreme Self, just like the objects of knowledge. Anticipating this, the author says: "Those who know the Vedas do not know Him"—meaning that neither the Vedas nor those who know them know Him, for they do not make Him an object of their cognition. He is beyond the reach of words.

One might object: "If that is so, how can Brahman be 'known through the Upaniṣads' (*aupaniṣada*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even though [it is so], they know it through the Veda"—that is, although Brahman is not an object of speech and the other senses, nevertheless, they know, that is, they understand, the Veda, which is the Supreme Self in the form of consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpa*), by means of the Veda, namely the *Ṛg-veda* and the others. Who are they? They are those Brāhmaṇas who are "knowers of the Veda," meaning those who know the manner in which the Vedas establish [the truth].

Anticipating the objection, "How then do the Vedas establish Brahman, which is indeed beyond the scope of objects? he says: "For the Vedas are like a portion of a part, just as branches belong to a tree.
The same applies even to consciousness; for they declare that when that [consciousness] is eternal, it is the very nature of the Supreme Self.

According to the Vedic revelation, "The moon is three watches [in diameter] for the sake of its one-watch portion," just as the branch of a tree becomes the cause for perceiving the digit of the moon on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*), so too do the Vedas become the causes for the eternal and imperishable consciousness—which is the very nature of the Supreme Self, the ultimate goal of man, and the form of perfect bliss—but they do not, however, directly express the Supreme Self which is beyond the reach of speech; thus they declare.

He who, having understood this method of explaining the Vedas as being the manifestation of the Self in the form of the Veda, explains them—he too is a Brāhmaṇa; thus he says: "I recognize the Brāhmaṇa as one who is an eloquent expounder.
He who understands in this way truly knows that which is supreme. (45)

I recognize as a wise Brāhmaṇa that expounder who explains the manner in which the Vedas set forth the nature of the Self. Now, one might object: since the text says "then he is a Brāhmaṇa" (*atha brāhmaṇaḥ*) with reference to one who has already transcended both childhood and scholarship, how can it be said, "I recognize as a Brāhmaṇa the wise expounder"? To this he replies: He who thoroughly understands this manner of explaining the Self—which consists of the knowledge of the Vedas as I have described it—he indeed knows; for he knows that which is supreme, namely, the Supreme Brahman. Thus it is.
The meaning is that he who, having become disillusioned with scholarship, remains steadfast, quickly becomes disillusioned with childhood and the rest, and thus becomes a Brahmin.

Since the status of being a true Brahmin is established only for one who is firmly rooted in truth, he says that one should not become dependent on external objects: "One should never go about seeking him among adversaries; by not searching for him in this Veda, one then beholds that Lord. (46)

"Objects, the senses, the body, and the ego—these are known as the terrible external and internal enemies of the yogin. Because of this teaching, one should not engage in "paryeṣaṇam"—that is, a pervasive seeking—among those adversaries and opponents of this Self, namely the body, the senses, and objects such as sound; the meaning is that one should not be intent on the pursuit of sense-objects. Without searching—that is, without accumulating sense-objects—one subsequently beholds this inner Self (pratyagātmānam) through the Vedas, specifically in the Upaniṣadic statements such as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi), and thereafter beholds Him, the Lord, the Supreme.

The meaning is that one knows the self as the self. Alternatively, the meaning is that one's search—that is, the investigation—of this self should not go toward adversaries, namely the body, the senses, and so forth, which act as its opposites; one should not grasp the body, the senses, and their attributes as the self.

Not investigating—that is, not collecting—the body, the senses, and their attributes as the Self, but instead attaining only the Self which is the witness of those very things, one perceives this Supreme Self, the witness of the knower and so forth, after the purification of the referents of the terms *tat* and *tvam*. The meaning is that, no longer perceiving the body, the senses, and their attributes as the Self, one perceives the Supreme Self as one's own Self through such statements as "That Thou Art" (*tattvamasi*).
One should attend [the teacher] in silence and not desire anything even with the mind;
through such repeated practice, Brahman will soon attain him in abundance. || 47 ||

Since the realization of the Self is achieved only through the renunciation of all objects, therefore, having become silent and performed the renunciation of all actions, having abandoned everything other than his own Self and becoming solitary, he should worship his own Self alone as the world; and he should not desire even with his mind—that is, he should not form a desire for sense-objects. For this silent Brahmin who, having withdrawn from sense-objects, worships his own Self alone as the world, Brahman—characterized by being without prior cause and so forth—will manifest before him.

In the *Sanatsujātīya-bhāṣya*, the meaning is that [the Self] becomes manifest. And it is heard in scripture: "He whom this [Self] chooses, by him is He attained; to him this Self reveals His own form. Subsequently, having become one whose true nature is manifested, he attains the Supreme Self—that which is the vastness of many, beyond darkness—this is the meaning.
"This very person is also a sage," he said; for one becomes a sage through silence, not by dwelling in the forest.
But he who knows that Imperishable is called the best of sages. (48)

One becomes a sage (*muni*) simply through silence—that is, from the state of being silent as previously described—and not merely by dwelling in the forest. Even among those who are silent, he who knows that imperishable syllable (*akṣara*), the Supreme Self, thinking "I am this," and knows it directly, is called the best of sages.

And it is heard in scripture: "Only by knowing this very one does one become a sage. He further states that this person alone is also a grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇa*): "He is called a grammarian because of his analysis (*vyākaraṇa*) of all objects;
for, based on that [knowledge], he analyzes grammar itself"—thus he is such.

One is called a *vaiyākaraṇa* (grammarian) because of the grammatical analysis (*vyākaraṇa*) of all things (*sarvārtha*), and not merely because of the grammatical analysis of a single portion of sound. Granted that one may be a *vaiyākaraṇa* through the analysis of all things, what follows from that? If it is asked this, the answer is: grammar has its root in that [Brahman], for from the previously mentioned syllable (*akṣara*) comes the analysis of the entire manifold of names and forms (*nāmarūpa-prapañca*). And it is heard in scripture: "Having entered with this living self (*jīva-ātman*), let me analyze names and forms. Therefore, Brahman alone is directly the *vaiyākaraṇa*.
"He explains it thus"—that is, this wise man also explains that Brahman in exactly that way; therefore, he is a "Vaiyākaraṇa" (an etymologist/expositor).
"He too is indeed omniscient," he said; "a man who perceives the worlds directly becomes all-seeing.
By abiding in the true Brahman, the knower of that indeed becomes all-knowing. (50)

He who is a direct seer of the worlds—one who perceives the worlds, beginning with the earth, through direct perception—becomes an all-seeing person; he beholds the Supreme Self in all its forms. Furthermore, abiding in Brahman, which is characterized by truth and other such qualities, he composes his mind. Knowing that—that is, knowing Brahman characterized by truth and so forth and realizing it as one's own self—he becomes all-knowing; the meaning is that he knows everything. Therefore, this alone is [the means]. (p. 283)

"He is the omniscient one himself, not merely one who perceives the non-self. With the words "But he who [is different] from these," etc., he shows once again the very same point already stated, for the purpose of demonstrating its necessity: "O Kṣatriya, even though established in knowledge and the rest, he thus perceives Brahman; I tell you this, O wise one, according to the conduct of the Vedas. (51)
Thus ends the second chapter of the Śrīmat Sanatsujātīya-bhāṣya.

Even while established in the qualities previously mentioned, such as knowledge and so forth—beginning with the words "and knowledge"—he perceives Brahman in this very manner, just as one who abides in truth perceives Brahman. This means that he does so preceded by the conduct of the Vedas, that is, preceded by the hearing of the Vedānta. Alternatively, this is an injunction regarding other qualities: even though he is established in knowledge and the rest, he does not perceive [Brahman] by that alone.

Rather, one perceives Brahman precisely in this manner—that is, preceded by the inquiry into the Vedānta, beginning with the hearing (*śravaṇa*) of the Vedānta texts. O learned one, I shall explain to you this method of inquiry into the Vedāntas; such is the intended meaning. Thus ends the second chapter of the *Sanatsujātīya-bhāṣya*.
The Third Chapter.
[p. 284] [p. 286] The Third Chapter.

Now, following the exposition of the means such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and so forth, the third and fourth chapters are commenced in order to establish that Brahman which is to be attained through them.

In this regard, having heard the teaching on the means such as celibacy and desiring knowledge of that Brahman, Dhṛtarāṣṭra says: Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: O Sanatsujāta, since you indeed speak these words concerning Brahman, which are for the sake of the Supreme and possess universal form—words that are exceedingly difficult to obtain regarding the highest goal—speak further to me, O Youth, according to your word. (1)

O Sanatsujāta, since you speak this speech related to Brahman (*brāhmī vāk*), which is for the sake of the Supreme, excellent in meaning, multiform, supreme, and most difficult to obtain even to hear among all worldly activities and their manifold expansions—therefore, O Youth, please declare such words to me. The intention is that because you speak this speech concerning Brahman, which is the means to achieve the highest human goal and is so very rare, you alone are worthy to speak it.
[287] Thus questioned, the Blessed One spoke; Sanatsujāta said: "O King, this Brahman about which you ask with such urgency and attachment cannot be attained by one who hastens.
For that knowledge, which must be contemplated within the intellect when the mind has dissolved, is indeed obtained through the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*)."

"This Brahman which you ask me about with such zeal, O King, is not to be attained by a person in a state of haste. How, then, is it to be attained? He says: when the mind has dissolved into the intellect (*buddhi*) characterized by determination, that knowledge is indeed to be contemplated. The meaning is this: when the mind—which consists of volition and doubt—turns away from sense objects and becomes motionless within its own self; that which is to be contemplated occurs when the mind has thus dissolved into the intellect.

That knowledge is to be obtained through the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) which will be described hereafter. Furthermore: "For you speak of that primordial knowledge which is of the nature of truth, which is attained by the virtuous through celibacy;
having attained which they cast off this mortal state—that knowledge which indeed resides eternally within teachers and elders. (3)
For you indeed speak of the primordial knowledge concerning Brahman, who is the source of all things, as being of the nature of truth;
thus ends the third chapter.

"Tell me that which has the nature of the ultimate truth. Or rather, you speak of that primordial knowledge (*vidyā*) which is not an effect and is not an object of the unreal phenomenal world (*asatya-prapañca*); therefore, the meaning is that it is attainable only by one who is unhurried, endowed with the means such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has been fully withdrawn.

That knowledge which is attained through celibacy by the virtuous, having attained which they cast off this mortal state—that knowledge which is constant and fixed among disciples who have been elevated by their teachers through the imparting of wisdom and other means—[is thus described]. Having spoken thus for the sake of understanding celibacy, Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: O learned one, tell me this: how may that celibacy be practiced, by which knowledge can be easily understood? (4)
How can that Brahman, which is the means by which the knowledge that is to be known through celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is attained, be ourselves? O Knower, tell me this regarding celibacy.

Thus questioned, the Blessed One Sanatsujāta replied: "Those who, having entered here the womb of the teacher and borne the embryo, practice celibacy—they become authors of the scriptures even in this world; casting off the body, they go to the supreme truth. (5)

“Those who, having entered the womb of the teacher”—that is, having gone into the presence of the teacher—and having become disciples through the rites of initiation (*upasadana*) and so forth, practice the life of a religious student (*brahmacarya*), such as service to the guru and the like, in this very world they become authors of the scriptures; that is, they become learned scholars (*paṇḍita*). Then, having become weary of childhood and other stages, and having become true Brahmins, they depart from the body upon the exhaustion of their commenced karma and go to the Supreme—the True One, characterized by reality (*satya*) and other such attributes—which is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
Moreover, in this world, those who endure the state of Brahman conquer their desires here;
they extract the self from the body in this life, as one draws the stalk from the muñja grass, by virtue of their steadfastness.

In this world, those who are victorious over their desires, who are seeking the state of Brahman—that is, the state established in Brahman itself—and who are practicing forbearance day by day, draw out the Self from the body, senses, and so forth; they extract that which is pure consciousness, the witness of all. How? Like a stalk from its sheaths; just as one extracts a stalk situated within its sheaths, so too, having drawn it out from the five sheaths, they realize the Universal Self. By what means? Through steadfastness—that is, by means of fortitude.

And it is heard in the Kaṭhavallīs: "The person the size of a thumb, the inner self, is always seated in the hearts of people. One should draw him out from one's own body with steadfastness, like a reed from its sheath; one should know him as the bright, immortal."
In the verse beginning with "The teacher is the source here," the status of the teacher as a source (*yoni*) is shown.

Anticipating the objection as to how the teacher can be a source apart from the mother and father, [the text] states that he is indeed the direct progenitor: "O Bhārata, these two—the father and the mother—produce the body;
but that birth which comes from the teacher is truly real and immortal."

In this world, these two—mother and father—produce only his body; they do not produce the Self in its true nature. This birth which consists of the two bodies is unreal. However, that birth which occurs through the teacher, by way of the Self that is Brahman—consciousness, existence, bliss, and non-dual—is real, the ultimate truth, and likewise immortal, being devoid of destruction. Therefore, the meaning is that he alone is the progenitor.

And it is heard in the *Praśna Upaniṣad*: "You indeed are our father, you who carry us across to the further shore of ignorance. Likewise, Āpastamba says: "For he (the teacher) procreates him through knowledge; that is the most excellent birth, whereas the mother and father produce only the physical body."
Since the attainment of the supreme goal of man depends upon the teacher, therefore: "He covers [the disciple] while bestowing immortality; for he knows that this has been done for him.
The disciple should always salute the guru and, remaining ever vigilant, desire the study of the Veda. (8)

One should not bear malice toward that teacher who does not conceal [the truth], but imparts the immortal, full-blissful Brahman as one's very self; one should not act with hostility toward him. Thus says the Śruti: "For one whose devotion to the Guru is as great as his devotion to the God, these meanings explained here shine forth for that high-souled one. Likewise, Āpastamba states: "One should never do anything harmful to him, for he indeed generates him from knowledge."

"Knowing what has been done by him"—here the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental—meaning, knowing the service rendered to himself by this [disciple]. What, then, ought he to do? He says: "He should always salute his teacher; he should attend upon the teacher as if he were a god. And thus says the Śruti: "One who has supreme devotion for the God, and likewise for the teacher as for the God..."

Likewise, one should desire self-study and always be intent upon hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, remaining vigilant and never negligent. Now, he describes the fourfold Brahmacarya in four verses, according to the sequence of the student’s conduct: "The pure one who attains knowledge through this very order of the student's conduct—this is called the first quarter of the vow of Brahmacarya. (9)

That celibacy (brahmacarya) by which one, being pure, attains knowledge through the very sequence of the student’s conduct— as described in the passage beginning with "The teacher is the source here"— is called its first quarter.
Just as one should always behave toward the guru, so should one behave toward the guru’s wife;
acting likewise toward his son, this is called the second quarter.

The meaning of this verse is clear. And so it has been said: "One's conduct toward the teacher's wife should be as toward the teacher; likewise, one's conduct toward the teacher's son should be as toward the teacher."

When the student recognizes what has been done for him by the teacher, and having recognized it, thinks, "I have been cultivated by this [teacher]," and feels a joyful mind toward him—that indeed is the third quarter of brahmacarya. || 11 ||

The third quarter of *brahmacarya* is that wherein one, recognizing the benefit performed for oneself by the teacher (*ācārya*), and having known and realized the meaning of the Vedas—that is, the supreme goal of human life—reflects, "I have been transformed by him; I have been truly produced as the self of Brahman, which is naturally consciousness, existence, bliss, and non-dual," and thus, with an intellect directed toward the teacher, considers himself to have achieved his purpose. This is the third quarter of *brahmacarya*.
One should do what is pleasing to the teacher even with one's life and wealth;
through action, mind, and speech—this is said to be the fourth quarter.
Now he shows the four-line vidyā: "In this way one obtains one quarter through time, and likewise one quarter through the yoga of the guru;
one shall attain one quarter through the yoga of enthusiasm, and from that, one proceeds to the quarter by means of the scripture."

In this context, the sequence is not intended to be emphasized. First, through association with a teacher; then, through the practice of *utsā* (exertion), by which a particular faculty of intelligence (*buddhi-viśeṣa*) manifests; then, through time, by the maturation of that intelligence; and then, through the scriptures, by means of inquiry into reality together with fellow students. Thus it has been said: "The student receives one quarter from the teacher, one quarter by his own intellect, one quarter through time, and one quarter from his fellow students."

He states that the attainment of the fruit occurs when knowledge and the other qualities are present in the proximity of a teacher: "Knowledge and the other eleven, whose form consists of these twelve, as well as the other limbs and likewise strength—these bear fruit through union with a teacher; and they call this 'brahmacarya' (the life of sacred study) because it is conjoined with the pursuit of Brahman. (14)

Regarding "knowledge and the rest": that person for whom the twelve qualities previously mentioned—beginning with "knowledge and"—constitute his form (*rūpa*), as well as the other limbs stated in the two verses beginning with "The sixfold renunciation is superior" and "Truth, meditation," as well as power (*bala*)—that is, the capacity to protect those dharmas—all of these bear fruit only through union with the Teacher (*ācārya-yoga*); they do not bear fruit without union with the Teacher. And it is heard in scripture: "Knowledge is truly known only from the Teacher," and "The person who has a Teacher knows."

And celibacy through union with the meaning of Brahman—that is, the practice of service and so forth in the presence of the Guru—this celibacy bears fruit through union with the meaning of Brahman; the meaning is that it bears fruit by way of accomplishing the oneness of one's own self with the non-dual Brahman, which is Consciousness, Being, and Bliss. He offers praise for celibacy in two verses: "By this celibacy, the gods attained godhood;
and the highly fortunate sages became [sages] through celibacy. (15)
By this very means, together with the Gandharvas, the Apsarases won their form;
by this celibacy, the Sun is born for the sake of the day.

By this [brahmacarya], the gods attained godhood; even the seers here attained the state of seers by this. Together with the Gandharvas—that is, existing together with the Gandharvas—the Apsarases conquered beauty; they conquered beautiful forms through this brahmacarya. And for the sake of the day—a mass of light—for the illumination of the worlds, the sun is born.
And it is said: "The light of the day is so described."
To the question of how a single practice of the religious life (*brahmacarya*) can accomplish manifold results, he says:
"Because it is conjoined with objects according to one's desire, as in the case of those seeking various flavors."

For it is by knowing this thus that these [gods and others] have attained such a state (tādṛgbhāva). Just as the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) and other such things bestow whatever object is desired through their connection with the object of desire for those seeking various essences (*rasabheda*), so too does this celibacy (*brahmacarya*) bestow whatever is desired through its connection with the object of desire. Having understood this, and having practiced celibacy for the sake of various fruits, these gods and others have attained such a state—that is, they have reached that very nature.

Since the attainment of the supreme goal of man results from the practice of celibacy performed in the presence of a teacher, the meaning is that one should enter the womb of the teacher and, having become an embryo, practice celibacy.

Now, one might object: "If steadfastness in knowledge were thus the goal of man, then knowledge alone would be the human end; however, it is action alone [that is so]. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "O Kṣatriya, the worlds won by action performed perish."

Through knowledge, the wise man constantly attains splendor; for otherwise, his path does not exist. (18) O Kṣatriya, they conquer finite worlds—such as the world of the ancestors and the world of the gods—but they do not conquer the infinite world, which is the Supreme Self, one's own true self. Anticipating the question, "By what means, then, is the attainment of the infinite world possible? he says: "Through knowledge. (p. 296)

The wise man constantly approaches that splendor; he constantly approaches that splendor which is the very self, imperishable, and luminous—not by action. Why, then, does he approach it only through knowledge? To this he says: "For otherwise, no other path exists for him. Indeed, apart from the single path of knowledge, there is no other way or road to that light of full bliss.
And it is heard in scripture: "Having known Him thus, one goes beyond death; no other path exists for the journey."

Regarding what the wise man perceives as Brahman through knowledge, Dhṛtarāṣṭra asked: Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Does it shine like white, or like red, or like black, or like white, or like brown? What is the form of that immortal, imperishable, supreme [reality] which a Brāhmaṇa perceives when he possesses knowledge? (19)

"What does that Brahman which the wise man perceives through knowledge appear like? Does it appear white, or does it appear red, or black, or pale, or tawny? In what place does it shine, and what is the form of that immortal, imperishable, supreme Brahman? Thus questioned, the venerable Sanatsujāta replied:
"It does not appear white, nor red, nor black, nor pale, nor tawny."
It does not stand upon the earth, nor in the atmosphere; it does not hold this water within the ocean.

This Brahman does not manifest as having a form such as white and so forth, because Brahman is formless. And it is heard in scripture: "That which is higher than that is formless and free from suffering," and "Without sound, without touch, without form. Likewise, it does not abide in the earth, nor in the intermediate space. Thus, scripture shows its non-abiding elsewhere: "In what, O Venerable One, is it established? In its own majesty."

For what reason, then, does it not abide in earth and the other elements? To this he says: "It does not bear the water in the ocean; it bears the body composed of the five elements. The word "water" (salila) is intended as an indicator for the pentad of elements (*bhūtapañcaka*). For example, in the passage, "He created the waters alone and deposited his seed in them," the word "waters" is an indicator for the pentad of elements. And it is heard in scripture: "In the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'"; thus, the waters alone are denoted by the term "man."

This is what is meant: if Brahman were to exist within the realm of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), then, by virtue of having entered into *saṃsāra*, it would possess such qualities as form and so forth, like a jar or similar objects, and would abide in something else. However, because its characteristics are "unprecedented" (*apūrva*) and so on, Brahman has not entered into *saṃsāra* at all. Therefore, it is indeed devoid of form and other such qualities.
"In that case, it would not be perceived anywhere at all," he said: "O King, it is not found in the Ṛg-verses, nor in the Yajus-formulas, nor even in the pure Sāman-chants;
whether in the Rathantara or the Vāmadevya, it is seen within the self of the Mahāvrata. (21)

Beginning with "Knowledge and Truth," and continuing with "The twelve great vows of the Brāhmaṇa," those qualities which have been described are seen within the Self of one endowed with them; that is the Supreme Brahman. It is not established as "this" in the manner of a jar or similar objects, but rather it is established as the Self within the Self itself—this is the meaning.
Now, by means of two verses, he points out its true nature, the vision thereof, and its fruit: "At the time of dissolution, it reaches the end [of all things], beyond darkness, being unobstructed;
its form is subtler than the subtlest, yet its essential nature is greater even than the mountains. (22)
All this exists as established therein; he who knows the Self perceives it all through the yoga of knowledge.
In the *Sanatsujātīya-bhāṣya*: "In this, this entire world is established; those who know this become immortal. (23)
Thus ends the third chapter in the venerable Sanatsujātīya.

That which is seen within the Great Vow (mahāvrata) is the unobstructed Brahman, because it has been fully understood. It is beyond darkness—that is, beyond ignorance. That Brahman reaches the end of the world at the time of dissolution, the time of universal destruction; it is of a subtle form, yet even subtler than the most subtle, and likewise possesses a magnitude greater than the greatest, even compared to mountains. And it is heard in scripture: "Subtler than the subtle, greater than the great."

And whatever things are seen in the world, such as minuteness, magnitude, and so forth—all this universe is established in Brahman during the day by means of the form of the day, which is the form of light; it shines by that very Self alone. It is heard in scripture: "By His light all this shines," and "By whose fiery splendor the sun burns. That Brahman is perceived by the knower of the Self through the yoga of knowledge, not through the yoga of action.
Upon that very Supreme Self, this entire universe is established. Those who know this become immortal. Thus ends the third chapter of the Śrī Sanatsujātīya-bhāṣya.
In the *Sanatsujātīya-bhāṣya*,
