The Fourth Chapter.

Having determined the nature of Brahman with the words, "That which is to be reached beyond darkness," and so forth, and having stated that the vision of the Self occurs through the yoga of knowledge in the passage, "Then those who know the Self behold [It] by means of the yoga of knowledge," [the text] again shows His essential form and declares that yogis behold that form: "That which is white, great light, blazing, and great glory—that which indeed the gods worship, from which the Unborn shines forth."
Yogis behold that eternal Blessed One. ||1||

That which the knower of Brahman perceives through the yoga of knowledge, knowing which they become immortal—that is the pure (śukram), the stainless, free from defects such as ignorance; it is the great light (mahaj-jyotiḥ) because it illumines everything. And it is heard in scripture: "By its light all this shines. It is shining, radiant, and of great glory (mahadyaśaḥ). And it is heard: "Its name is great glory. That very Brahman which the gods, Indra and the others, worship. And it is heard: "The gods worship that light of lights as life, as immortality. (p. 303)

Thus it is said: because the sun, the *arka*, shines by the light of the Supreme Brahman—as the Śruti declares, "By whose fiery energy the sun burns"—only yogis behold such a Supreme Self, the Blessed One, the Eternal; those devoid of the yoga of knowledge do not.
Now, he shows the origin of Hiraṇyagarbha and others from the Supreme Brahman alone: "From the seed (śukra) Brahman originates; Brahman grows by means of the seed.
That seed, in the midst of the luminaries, burns intensely as the burner."

Yogis behold that eternal Blessed One. From the pure [śukra] previously mentioned, from Brahman, that which is called Hiraṇyagarbha arises; thus Brahman is born. Then, once born, that Brahman increases by means of the pure [śukra] through the form of Virāj. That pure Brahman, in the midst of the luminaries such as the sun and others, being unillumined (atapram) by them, shines by itself alone, heating and illuminating even them.
Only yogins behold that Blessed One who, being unmanifest to others, is the illuminator of all and shines by himself alone.
Now he declares the full meaning of the statement: "From the Full they draw forth the Full; from the Full they declare the Full to be;
they take away the Full from the Full, yet by the Full alone it remains."
Yogis behold that eternal Blessed One. ||3||

From the Supreme Self, which is full and undivided in terms of space, time, and substance, they draw forth that which is indeed full in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*). Since that which is full has been drawn forth from the Full as the individual self, the wise declare that this very nature of the individual soul is also full, precisely because it has been drawn forth from the Full.

In this way, they carry away the full [beings] who abide as the individual self (*jīvātman*). The meaning is that, having extracted from the body and senses that which is the full nature of the Self alone—which had entered into the body, senses, and so forth—the innermost witness within all is drawn out from the two bodies. Then, by means of that very root-essence of full bliss which has been thus extracted, one remains; that is to say, one becomes united with that very Brahman of full bliss and abides in the nature of Brahman, which is consciousness, existence, bliss, and non-dual.

Alternatively, there is the reading: "Only the Full remains. This means that when one extracts the Witness of all, who is the innermost Self, from the body, senses, and so forth, and draws Him out from the two bodies, then only the Full remains. Thus says the Śruti: "Full is That; full is this. From the Full, the Full arises. When the Full is taken from the Full, only the Full remains. The meaning of this is as follows: "Full is That" refers to Brahman, the cause of the universe, denoted by the word *tat* (That). "Full is this" points to the nature of the inner Self (*pratyagātman*), indicated by the word *idam* (this).

If it is asked how these two referents of the terms *tat* and *tvam* possess fullness (*pūrṇatva*), he says in response: "Because from that which is full, unconditioned, and undivided, the full alone is emitted—that is, it overflows—in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), therefore these two possess fullness. This means that by taking the full form of the Reality (*tattva*) which exists as the Self, one performs the purification of the referents of the terms *tat* and *tvam*; having thus purified the referents of the terms, only the full Brahman remains—only the full Brahman [remains].

The meaning is that [He] exists. Only yogis perceive that Supreme Self who is of a perfect nature. Now, he explains the meaning of the mantra "dvā suparṇā": "The waters, and then another, the ocean—in the midst of that, both gods have taken refuge in the intermediate space.
Wearing [garments] directed downward and upward, He supports both the earth and the sky."
Yogis behold that eternal Blessed One.

From this Supreme Self, water was created first; thus Manu says: "In the beginning, he created water alone. The word "water" (āpaḥ) is intended as an illustration for the pentad of elements. By this, the subtle creation has been described. Then, immediately after that, from the previously created waters, the gross body and so forth—consisting of the pentad of elements—was created, known as "salila."

Within that water, which exists as both body and self, in the intermediate space—that is, in the space of the heart—both gods, Jīva and Paramātman, whose nature is luminosity, have taken refuge and abide. They do not abide in the intermediate space alone; rather, they dwell "clad in the *ādhīcya*s and the *saviṣūcya*s. The directions facing toward oneself are called *ādhīcya* because they are held or situated facing [the center]. The intermediate directions (*upadiś*) are called *viṣūcya* because they extend in all directions (*viṣvak*); those together with them are the *saviṣūcya*s, namely the eastern and other primary directions. [p. 306]

Clothing and covering all directions, the one living soul (jīva) sustains both the earth and the heaven. Having failed to realize the secondless reality of the Self—the Brahman which is by nature consciousness and eternal bliss—that single soul has fallen into the notion of selfhood within the non-self, such as the body and so forth; thus it sustains the "earth," characterized by the elements and their derivatives, consisting of bodies of pleasure and pain corresponding to the fruits of karma. The other [the Supreme Self] sustains the "heaven," which is its own luminous essential nature.

And it is heard in scripture: "Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree. Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating. He who, by His own *māyā*, having divided Himself into the infinite variety of vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, enters within and remains beholding—all yogis behold that Blessed One.

Now he shows the abiding of the knower within his own self: "The horses carry him, who possesses banners, who stands upon the wheel of the chariot—of the fixed one whose action is imperishable—that divine, undecaying [Self] in heaven."
Yogis behold that eternal Blessed One.

In the wheel—which consists of the movement of the body that exists as the three worlds—of the chariot which is the body of the Supreme Lord, who is eternal and whose activity is imperishable, and who abides as the Self of the Lord, there stands one who possesses a banner, that is, who is endowed with wisdom; and for that very reason, he is divine, non-material, free from old age, death, and the like, and shines in the heaven (*divi*) which is of the nature of light.

The senses (*indriyāṇi*) are the horses moving toward Brahman, which abides as the self of tranquilized knowledge and full bliss. This is what is meant: although the senses by their very nature operate only toward external objects, nevertheless, when drawn by the charioteer of discernment (*vijñāna*), they carry one toward the Person who has the banner (the supreme goal), and not toward external objects. Thus it is said in the *Kaṭhavallīs*: "Know the Self as the rider in the chariot, and the body indeed as the chariot."

"Know the intellect (*buddhi*) to be the charioteer and the mind (*manas*) to be the reins; they say the senses are the horses, and the objects of the senses are their paths. The wise say that the Self (*ātman*), when joined with the senses and the mind, is the enjoyer. And so forth. Only yogis behold that Blessed One in whom [the senses] flow through austerity. He says that nothing exists equal to Him: "His form does not stand within the range of comparison; no one sees Him with the eye.
But those who know Him by means of wisdom (*manīṣā*), and by the mind and the heart, they become immortal."
Yogis behold that eternal Blessed One.

The form of this Supreme Self does not abide in similarity; it does not exist in likeness with anything else, meaning that nothing exists which is similar to it. And it is heard in scripture: "There is no image of Him whose name is Great Glory. Therefore... [p. 308]

Thus, [the Self] is not an object of comparison and so forth. Likewise, no one perceives this Supreme Self, which is within all, with the eye. How, then, do they perceive It? By means of *manīṣā*—that is, by the mind characterized by determination—and by the *hṛt*, that is, the heart characterized by volition and conceptualization, serving as the instrument. Thinking that the perception of the Supreme Self is not possible without the heart, it is said: "and by the heart."

Or rather, not only by means of the mind and intellect, but being favored also by the heart and by the Supreme Lord residing within the heart—those who know this Supreme Self, thinking "I am He," they become immortal, possessing the nature of immortality.

Alternatively, "by the heart" (*hṛdā*) means by the heart, that is, by the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Accordingly, when the Supreme Self resides in the heart, the word "heart" is etymologically explained: "This very Self is in the heart; its etymology is this: 'He is in the heart' (*hṛdi ayam*), therefore it is called 'the heart' (*hṛdayam*); indeed, one who knows thus goes day after day to the heavenly world. Likewise, scripture shows that the realization of the Self is dependent upon Him: "For him who has supreme devotion for the Divine, and as for the Divine so for the Guru, these truths declared here shine forth to that great-souled one."
Thus, having known that by which they become immortal, only the yogis perceive it.
Now, he says that the engagement of the senses with their objects leads to misfortune: "The twelve hosts, protected by the gods, feast upon the rivers of honey;
following after them, they then wander into the terrible [realm]. Yogins behold him, the eternal Blessed One."

In the *Sanatsujātīya-bhāṣya*, it is said that there are twelve groups (*pūga*): the eleven organs of action and knowledge, with the mind (*manas*) as the eleventh and the intellect (*buddhi*) as the twelfth. With respect to many persons, each one of these is called a "group. The rivers are characterized by their constant flowing; they are "protected by the Divine" (*devarakṣitāḥ*), meaning protected by the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). They "rule over the honey" (*madhu*)—that is, the sense-objects—like honey; the meaning is that they experience their respective objects without confusion, exercising control over them.

When they experience things in this manner, then, following after them, those intent on sense-objects wander through the terrible cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). Therefore, the meaning is that one should withdraw the senses from their objects and bring them under control within one's own self. Only yogis behold that God by whom, when protected, [the senses] do not transgress.
Furthermore, there is the statement regarding the illustration and the illustrated therein: "The bee drinks the honey accumulated over half a month;
the Lord has ordained [the sacrificial] oblation to exist within all beings."

Yogis behold that eternal Blessed One. Just as a honey-gathering bee drinks for half a month the honey it has gathered and accumulated over the previous half-month, so too this "bee"—the transmigrating soul (saṃsārī)—because of its wandering nature, drinks for half a month the honey pertaining to that [former] object which was accumulated during the [previous] half-month; that is to say, it experiences in one birth the karma accumulated in a previous birth.

The accomplishment of the fruit from an action that bears fruit in this life may indeed occur, because it follows immediately after the action; but how, then, could there be the accomplishment of the fruit from an action that bears fruit in the hereafter, given the cessation of the action?

Anticipating the objection that [the result] would perish, he says: "The Lord. This defect would indeed arise if the accomplishment of the fruit were to come from action alone; however, the Lord, the Supreme Sovereign, depending upon the effort exerted, has ordained food and other offerings for all living beings—both for the Prāṇāgnihotra and other rites—in accordance with their respective actions. Only yogis behold that Blessed One who, as the Lord, has ordained the offering within all beings.

Furthermore, raising the doubt as to whether these bees, while wandering about, merely continue to revolve forever consuming honey, or whether they attain knowledge and become liberated, [the Lord] says: "Having flown toward the golden-leaved Aśvattha tree, those wingless ones become possessed of wings there and fly away according to their pleasure."
Yogis behold that eternal Blessed One. ||9||

Those who are "without wings"—meaning those devoid of the wing of knowledge—and who wander about as "honey-eaters," they fly toward the golden-leaved *aśvattha* tree, which is both beneficial (*hita*) and delightful (*ramaṇīya*). Thus, it is that *aśvattha* whose leaves are golden, beneficial, and delightful. And so says the Lord Vāsudeva: "Whose leaves are the Vedic meters. Having flown toward and ascended that golden-leaved *aśvattha*, the meaning is that they attain the bodies of Brāhmaṇas and others who are connected with the Vedas.

In that very state, having become wise birds within the bodies of Brahmins and others, they fly forth; thus says the Brāhmaṇa: "Those who are indeed wise are winged; those who are ignorant are wingless. The meaning is that they fall [into liberation] and thereby become liberated in happiness. Having known that [Reality], they fly forth. [p. 311]
Only yogins perceive that. Now he demonstrates yoga: "The prāṇa swallows the apāna; the moon swallows the prāṇa;
the sun swallows the moon; the Supreme swallows the sun."
Yogis behold that eternal Blessed One.

The vital breath (prāṇa) swallows and withdraws the downward breath (apāna). The mind (manas) swallows and withdraws the vital breath; the moon is the presiding deity of the mind, therefore the mind is referred to by the word "moon. The sun, which is the intellect (buddhi), swallows that moon, which is the mind.

The sun is the presiding deity of the intellect (*buddhi*). That Supreme Brahman swallows that sun, which is the intellect. This is what is meant: at the time of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), having withdrawn the *apāna* into the *prāṇa*, the *prāṇa* into the mind (*manas*), the mind into the intellect, and the intellect into the Supreme Self, one remains established as the very nature of the Self—which is Brahman, consisting of consciousness, existence, bliss, and non-duality. This is the meaning.

Now he shows the state of the Supreme as the individual soul (jīvātman): "The swan, rising from the water, does not lift one foot; if it were to lift that [foot] constantly, there would be neither death nor immortality."
Yogis behold that eternal Blessed One.

It destroys ignorance and its effects; thus it is the *haṃsa*, the Supreme Self. Emerging from the "water"—that is, from the cycle of transmigration characterized by the elements and their derivatives—it moves upward, remaining entirely outside of saṃsāra.

It does not lift up, nor does it extract, nor does it withdraw its single foot called the individual soul (*jīva*); the meaning is that it remains as a reflection corresponding to every form. And it is heard in the *Kaṭhavallīs*: "In the same way, the one Inner Self of all beings."

Why, then, does he not lift up even one foot? To this he says: If He were to lift up that foot called the *jīva*—which is constantly and continuously moving—and by His own *māyā* were to divide His own Self into infinite forms such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, and having entered into them, were not to abide as the individual soul (*jīvātman*), then there would be no death; that is, there would be no misfortune characterized by birth and death, namely, *saṃsāra*, because of the absence of the transmigrating *jīva*.

Likewise, immortality—the state of being immortal, which is liberation—would not exist for one who has not entered [into it], because seeing [the Truth] is impossible for such a person. And thus, for that very purpose, he shows the entry with the words, "Form after form. Likewise, there is this Vedic scripture: "The swan, rising from the water, does not lift one foot."

"If he were to lift his foot, there would be neither death nor immortality," and "He who makes the one form manifold. Only yogis perceive that Supreme Self, who abides as the individual soul (jīvātman) in the form of a quarter-foot and as the Brahman-self—which is consciousness, existence, bliss, and non-dual—in the form of three quarters.

Anticipating the question, "By what limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) does the Supreme abide as the individual self (*jīvātman*)?", he shows that the individual self is none other than the Supreme when conditioned by the subtle body (*liṅga*): "The person (*puruṣa*) the size of a thumb is the inner self; through its connection with the subtle body, it moves eternally.
Fools do not see that Lord—the primordial, the one to be worshipped, the source of all creation—who shines forth. [p. 313]
Yogis behold that eternal Blessed One.

That very one—the inner self who is existence-consciousness-bliss, non-dual, the inner self of all beings, the Supreme Person, the full Supreme Self—becoming limited by the measure of a thumb through the connection with the subtle body (liṅga), wanders and transmigrates eternally.

For what reason, then, does that which is the size of a thumb transmigrate by means of connection with the subtle body (*liṅga*)? To this he says: He who, through connection with the subtle body, transmigrates as one the size of a thumb—he is the Lord (*īśa*), the ruler of all, the one worthy of praise (*īḍya*), the one to be extolled. Having entered into every subsequent manifestation (*anukalpa*), he fashions it by himself; thus he is "the subsequent fashioner" (*anukalpa*). Because the deluded, the undiscriminating—who identify the two bodies as the Self—do not perceive him as the "first" (*ādya*), existing from the beginning, the "Virāj," the shining and radiant one, therefore, due to their failure to realize the Self's nature as Brahman, they transmigrate.

...thus they say. Only yogins perceive that Self which those who do not see wander through the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). Now, he shows how both the sense-faculties and their objects are causes of misfortune: Like serpents in their holes, they hide themselves by leading mortals to their destruction through their own conduct.
When those deluded people emerge, the enjoyments bestowed by them delude them toward further existence (*bhava*).
Yogis behold that eternal Blessed One.

Just as serpents, having emerged from their holes, lead mortals to destruction by means of their own behavior—the delivery of poison—and then hide themselves within those very holes, concealing their own nature; even so, the serpents that are the senses, lying dormant in the ears and other organs, emerge from the ears and so forth, lead mortals to destruction by means of their own behavior—the delivery of the poison of sense-objects—and then hide themselves within those holes, concealing their own nature.

Overcome by the poison of the sense-objects, they become utterly deluded; the meaning is that they are so bewildered that they know nothing beyond them. And thus says the Śruti: "As one embraced by a beloved wife... The enjoyments provided by those enemies, the senses, are like poison; these objects delude mortals and repeatedly become causes of delusion. This delusion caused by sense-objects leads to *bhava*, that is, to the cycle of worldly existence consisting of conception, birth, old age, and death.

Those blinded by the poison of sense-objects do not perceive that which is blameless, faultless, the primordial ritual alternative, and they become deluded; only the yogins behold it. Regarding the nature of liberation for the wise, he says: "Whether without means or with means, this is seen to be the same among human beings;
this is the same for the immortal and the other. The disciplined ones have reached the spring of honey therein."
Yogis behold that eternal Blessed One.

Among those who are "without means"—devoid of the means such as tranquility (*śama*) and self-control (*dama*)—and those who are "with means," endowed with the means such as tranquility and self-control, the nature of the Self is seen to be common and shared among human beings. Likewise, regarding immortality—that is, liberation (*mokṣa*)—whether it exists or does not exist [among others], those among them who are "joined," meaning endowed with the means such as tranquility and self-control, have reached the spring of honey (*madhva utsam*) in that supreme abode of Viṣṇu; the meaning is that they attain Brahman, which is full bliss.

Only yogis behold that which the disciplined attain—the fullness of supreme bliss. Moreover, they go pervading both worlds through knowledge; thus, the Agnihotra sacrifice becomes both offered and unoffered. Let not your Brahmanic wisdom bring about insignificance; let it be called true discernment, for the steadfast alone obtain it.
Yogis behold that eternal Blessed One.

Having pervaded both worlds—the world of this life and the world beyond—with the knowledge whose object is the identity of Brahman and the Self, he goes to that Brahman which is full bliss. Because he goes having pervaded both worlds with knowledge, therefore even the *ahuta* (unoffered) Agnihotra becomes *āhuta* (fully offered) by means of this knowledge of the Self; the meaning is that the entire fruit of ritual acts such as the Agnihotra is accomplished by this alone.

Since one traverses both worlds by means of knowledge, and since even an unoffered *agnihotra* becomes as if offered, therefore let not your *brāhmī*—pertaining to Brahman—knowledge incur lightness or the state of mortality like ritual action; rather, it brings about the realization of the Supreme Self as one's own self, which is wisdom (*prajñāna*), the further shore beyond darkness. For when one who is engaged in the knowledge of Brahman realizes the Supreme Self as one's own self, that which is named "wisdom" is indeed Brahman.

This is the meaning. And thus says the Śruti: "Brahman is consciousness" (*prajñānaṃ brahma*). Wise, intelligent people attain that Brahman which is consciousness. Only those who are practitioners of yoga (*yogin*) behold that Brahman which the wise attain. Furthermore: "The Great Self of such a nature swallows the Puruṣa as fire; indeed, for one who knows that Puruṣa, his self is not harmed in this world."
Yogis behold that eternal Blessed One.

He who thus abides as one whose very nature is Brahman, consisting of the single essence of wisdom—that Self becomes great; the meaning is that he becomes Brahman itself. He who knows that Person—the one whose sole essence is knowledge, the full one, dwelling in the city (the body)—as the fire that consumes, as the cause that withdraws all effects along with their causes into its own self—he indeed [is this].

One directly knows "I am He"; for him who realizes the Supreme Self, whose nature is pure consciousness, as his own self, the Self does not suffer harm nor perish in this very body, because for the knower there is no departure (utkrānti), and destruction is caused by such departure.

And thus the Śruti, by means of a question, demonstrates the absence of departure: "Do the vital breaths (prāṇas) depart from him, or not? "No," said Yājñavalkya, "they are merged right here; his prāṇas do not depart. Being Brahman, he attains Brahman—he who knows thus. And: "Knowing which one does not perish—only yogis see that [Self]. Since there is no destruction of the Self through the knowledge of That, therefore it is always honored as the existent; for where there is no death, how could there be immortality?"
Truth and falsehood are both connected to truth; they are the single source of both the existent and the non-existent.
Yogis behold that eternal Blessed One.

He who always, at all times, day and night, is honored—that is, he who identifies himself with the non-dual Brahman as being of the nature of Existence-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda)—he is forever honored. For him there shall be no death; that is, the cycle of worldly existence characterized by birth and death shall not occur. How could there be immortality? Since immortality is dependent upon its opposite, death, in the absence of the latter, how could the former even arise? And so it is said [p. 318]:

The Śruti says: "Death does not exist; whence could there be immortality? Both truth and falsehood exist as being connected with truth; they proceed by clinging to the one ultimate reality (paramārtha-satya) as their substratum, just as a snake [appears] upon a rope.

How is it understood that "truth and falsehood are bound to truth"? To this he says: since they declare that the one non-dual Brahman alone is the source—that is, the cause—of both the existent (the empirical world) and the non-existent (such as illusory silver in worldly transaction), therefore truth and falsehood are bound to the truth that constitutes their own cause. Only yogis perceive that reality from which the destruction of death arises, and to which truth and falsehood are bound as they proceed.
The Person, the size of a thumb, is the inner self; though seated within the heart, he is not seen.
He is unborn, moving day and night without weariness; having realized him, the wise man remains serene.

Having created the universe from space down to the body, the Unborn One, who is the self of all that is moving and unmoving, has entered within the heart; yet he is not perceived by his own Self, which is consciousness, existence, bliss, and non-dual. Therefore, becoming untiring day and night, the wise man emerges from the five sheaths, realizes the Innermost Self of all, and remains serene, having attained his goal—this is the meaning.
From that the wind arose, and in that same place its dissolution occurs;
from that came both fire and the moon, and from that the vital breath (prāṇa) emerged.
In the *Sanatsujātīya-bhāṣya*: "That is the foundation; that is the immortal; those are the worlds; that is Brahman; that is glory.
From it all beings were born, and into it they go at the time of dissolution."

It has been stated in two verses that all this has arisen from Brahman and is dissolved back into Him; He now explains that very point: "The two gods, the earth and the sky, and the quarters, as well as the bright world—all these He sustains.
From Him the quarters and the rivers flow; from Him the great oceans are ordained. (21)
The meaning of the verse is clear.

Now he describes the infinity of Brahman: Even if one were to gather thousands upon thousands of wings and fly away with them, one would not reach the end of the Cause, even if one possessed the speed of thought.
Yogis behold that eternal Blessed One.

Suppose a person were to take a thousand times a thousand feathers and, having attached them to himself, fly for many millions of kalpas; even so, that person would not reach the end of the Cause, the Supreme Self who is the cause of all. Even if he possessed the speed of thought, he still would not reach its end. Because one cannot reach its end, therefore the Supreme Self is infinite (ananta). Only yogis perceive that Supreme Self who is infinite.
Moreover: "While remaining in invisibility, they see His form; those beings who are well-kindled [by austerity] behold Him.

The wise one, humbled, should perceive Him with the mind; those who know Him thus become immortal. (23) "While remaining in invisibility"—that is, in a state that is not an object fit for visual perception—He remains as the form of this Supreme Self.

And so says the Śruti: "His form does not stand within the range of vision. Even though He stands beyond the possibility of being seen, those whose inner being (*sattva*) is well-kindled behold this Supreme Self. Who are they? Those whose inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is "well-kindled"—that is, thoroughly and perfectly ignited by means of purification through sacrifices and other such practices—are those whose *sattva* is well-kindled.

Since this is so, therefore the wise person—lowly in the sense of being free from passion, hatred, and other impurities, and thus a pure being—should perceive with the mind: "I am he. Those who know this Supreme Self as "I am He" become immortal, possessing the nature of immortality.
He who perceives the Self in all beings,
wherever they are joined in various states— what could he grieve for beyond that?

He who perceives this Self as the innermost essence within all beings and all living creatures—perceiving it as what? Within those various bodies, senses, and so forth, which are characterized by the conceit of being the body and its attributes—he, seeing his own Self in all beings, what would he grieve for thereafter? Having seen the Self abiding in all beings, what further cause for lamentation remains? The meaning is that, because his purpose is fulfilled, he does not grieve. Thus says the Śruti: "In that state, what delusion, what sorrow can there be for one who perceives oneness?"
He says that very thing: "Just as in a great reservoir where water has overflowed on all sides, so it is with respect to all beings, and especially toward a Brāhmaṇa. (25)

Just as for one who has accomplished all his purposes there is no further need at a great reservoir where water overflows from every side, so too for the Brahmin who perceives the Self in all beings, there exists no purpose whatsoever; this is the meaning. And thus the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva said: "And he has no dependence on any object among all beings."
Now, in order to strengthen the meaning already stated, he demonstrates his own direct experience, like Vāmadeva and others: "I alone am your mother; I am the father, and again, I am the son.
I am the Self of all—both that which does not exist and that which exists."
O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, I alone am your mother, the progenitor;

I am also your father. I am your son, Duryodhana and the others. What more need be said? I am the Self (ātman) of all living beings—of that which exists and that which does not exist; I alone am their Self. Thus far, the paternal and other relationships on the level of the physical world (ādhibhautika) have been shown. Now, He shows the state of being the father and so forth on the level of the divine (ādhidaivika): "I am the ancient Grandfather, the Father, and the Son, O Bhārata."
"You abide within my very self; yet you do not belong to me, nor do I belong to you."

I am the Grandfather—the ancient, aged one who is the grandfather of Indra and the other gods; that beginningless, established Supreme Self is also none other than I. He who is the father of Indra and the others, Hiraṇyagarbha, is also none other than I. Likewise, you are all situated within my very self. Thus, in the ultimate sense, you are all not established within my self, nor am I established within you. And so the Blessed Lord has said: "All beings are situated in Me."

Although you are not established within me, nor am I established within you, nevertheless, the Self alone is my abode and the Self is my birth; I am woven through and through by the Self, established in the ageless.
As the unborn Lord, unwearied day and night, the sage who knows me remains serene. [p. 323] 28.
Smaller than the smallest, benevolent, and abiding within all beings, they know him as the father of all beings, established in the lotus. 29.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled the Śrīmatsanatsujātīya, within the Dhṛtarāṣṭra-Sanatkumāra-saṃvāda of the Udyogaparvan, in the Śatasāhasrī Saṃhitā composed by Vyāsa, from the glorious Mahābhārata.

The Self alone is the place, the Self alone is the support, and the Self is the birth; from this very Self everything has arisen. And so says the Śruti: "The Self alone is all this. I alone am woven across and through (otaprota), established in the form of the warp and woof of the universe. I am the Self of the world, your progenitor, established in the undecaying (ajara). "Established in the undecaying" means that He abides in His own majesty which is free from old age and death.
And so says the Śruti: "In what, O Blessed One, is He established? In His own majesty—or perhaps not even in majesty."

Subtler than the subtle (*aṇoḥ aṇīyān*), he is "well-minded" (*sumanāḥ*); that is, one whose mind (*manas*) is auspicious—beautifully free from qualities such as passion, hatred, pride, envy, grief, and delusion—and consists solely of the form of the Brahman-Self, which is consciousness, existence, bliss, and non-dual. [He perceives this] in all beings, in all living creatures...

"Within the lotus of the heart, I alone am established as the Self. Thus far, his own experience has been shown. Now, it is said that not only is our own experience the authority here, but others also understand it in this very way: "They know the Father of all beings to be seated in the lotus."

Other knowers of Brahman, such as Sanaka, Sanandana, Vāmadeva, and others, also know Him—the Supreme Lord who is the father, the progenitor, of all beings and all living creatures—to be seated in the *puṣkara*, that is, in the middle of the heart-lotus; the meaning is that they realize the Supreme Self as their own self.

And thus scripture shows their experience: "Seeing this very [Self], the seer Vāmadeva realized, 'I was Manu and I was the Sun,'" in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad; and "He sits singing this Sāman," in the Taittirīyaka, where his own experience is shown through the singing of the Sāman for the purpose of manifesting the fulfillment of his purpose as the Self. Likewise, in the Chāndogya it says, "Then he understood it from him"; and in the Talavakāra, the experience of the knower is shown by the words, "I am food," and so forth.

In this regard, there are these verses: Meditating upon the Lord as one whose nature is eternally pure, awakened, and liberated, and being motionless, he should thoroughly restrain the six sense organs. (1)
There exists a reality, a mass of consciousness, which is the cause of the world's birth;
it is not perishable, and it dispels the darkness of that world which arises from it.
Thus [it is said].
That which is the singular denotation of that state, eternally immortal and stainless, the bliss perceived through the cessation of mental fluctuations—that I am, that I am. (3)

Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Śrīmat-Sanatsujātīya-Bhāṣya*, composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavat-pūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering mendicant teacher (*paramahaṃsa-parivrājakācārya*). Thus the *Śrīmat-Sanatsujātīya-Bhāṣya* is complete.
